m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Check that your computer and browser can run Teachable Machine.
  • Start an image project and name the three panels you'll use all course.
  • Allow camera access on Windows, macOS, or a Chromebook, and fix it when it's blocked.
  • Explain where your samples are stored and what would make them leave your computer.

In the next lesson your laptop will learn to tell a thumbs-up from a thumbs-down. It will take about five minutes, it won't need a line of code, and the "learning" will happen inside one browser tab while you watch.

The tool that makes this possible is Teachable Machine, a free website from Google. You show it examples, it trains a small machine learning model on them, and then it tries to recognize new things you show it. We'll use it all course long to test ideas for real instead of just reading about them: why a model fails on a new background, why more examples help, why a perfect score can be a lie.

This lesson gets it running and makes sure you understand what happens to the pictures you take.

#What you need (and what you don't)

  • A laptop or desktop computer. Windows, Mac, and Chromebook all work. The training screen is built for a full-size screen.
  • Chrome or Firefox. Edge and Safari open the site too, but Teachable Machine itself recommends Chrome or Firefox, and its sound projects work best there.
  • A webcam (built in or USB). It's optional: every image project can also be trained from photo files you upload, so a phone camera plus a way to move photos to your computer is enough.
  • A microphone for the sound project in Module 2. Most laptops have one built in.

You do not need an account, a download, an install, or any money. Teachable Machine's own FAQ says it plainly: go to the site, click Get Started, and there's no need to log in.

📝 Note

Some lessons include short Python programs that draw charts. You don't need to read or run them. The chart, and the explanation under it, is the point.

#Start your first project

  1. Open Chrome or Firefox and go to teachablemachine.withgoogle.com.
  2. Click Get Started. The New Project screen shows three cards: Image Project, Audio Project, and Pose Project.
  3. Click Image Project. You'll be asked to pick a model type.
  4. Choose Standard image model ("Best for most uses"). The other option, Embedded image model, makes tiny greyscale models for microcontrollers. We never need it.

The project page opens. On a first visit, little boxes labeled 1. Gather Samples, 2. Train your Model, and 3. Export your model point at the three parts of the screen. They're the whole workflow in three steps:

Classes (left). Each card is one category you want the model to learn, like "Thumbs up". A card starts with the label Add Image Samples: and two buttons, Webcam and Upload. Click the pencil next to "Class 1" to rename it. Add a class at the bottom makes another card.

Training (middle). The Train Model button turns your examples into a model. Under it, Advanced hides settings called Epochs, Batch Size, and Learning Rate. Leave them alone for now; Module 4 explains what each one does.

Preview (right). Until you train, it says "You must train a model on the left before you can preview it here." After training, it shows a live camera view and a bar for each class showing how strongly the model leans toward that class.

#Let Teachable Machine use your camera

Click Webcam on the Class 1 card. Your browser asks whether the site may use your camera. In Chrome, choose Allow while visiting the site (or Allow this time). In Firefox, click Allow. A live view of you appears inside the card with a Hold to Record button under it.

That's success. If instead you see "There was an error opening your webcam. Make sure permissions are enabled or switch to image uploading," the camera is blocked somewhere. There are two places it can be blocked: the browser, and the computer itself.

Windows

In the browser. In Chrome, open the three-dot menu, then Settings › Privacy and security › Site settings › Camera. If teachablemachine.withgoogle.com is listed under "Not allowed", click it and change Camera to Allow. Reload the page.

In Windows 11. Open Start › Settings › Privacy & security › Camera. Turn on Camera access and Let desktop apps access your camera. Chrome and Firefox count as desktop apps, so the second switch is the one people miss.

In Windows 10. Open Start › Settings › Privacy › Camera. Make sure camera access for this device is on, then turn on Allow desktop apps to access your camera.

If a switch is greyed out, a school or family administrator controls it, and you'll need to ask them.

macOS

In the browser. In Chrome, open the three-dot menu, then Settings › Privacy and security › Site settings › Camera and allow teachablemachine.withgoogle.com. In Firefox, click the camera icon at the left of the address bar and clear the block. Reload the page.

In macOS. Open the Apple menu, then System Settings › Privacy & Security › Camera (on older Macs: System Preferences › Security & Privacy › Privacy › Camera). Turn on the switch for your browser. macOS will ask you to quit and reopen the browser; do it, or the change won't apply.

Chromebook

In the browser. Open the three-dot menu, then Settings › Privacy and security › Site settings › Camera, and allow teachablemachine.withgoogle.com. Reload the page.

In ChromeOS. Newer Chromebooks also have a system-wide switch. Open Settings › Privacy and security › Privacy controls and turn on Camera access (and Microphone access while you're there, for Module 2). Some Chromebooks also have a physical camera switch or slider on the side; check that it's on.

School Chromebooks are often managed by the school. If the camera is blocked and you can't change it, use Upload with photo files instead. Every activity in this course works that way.

⚠️ Watch out

The camera works in other sites but not here. Another app is probably holding it. Video-call apps (Zoom, Teams, Meet, FaceTime) keep the camera busy even when minimized. Quit them completely, then reload Teachable Machine. If it still fails, restart the browser.

#Where your pictures go, and what would make them leave

This is worth knowing before you point a camera at your bedroom. Teachable Machine's FAQ makes three clear promises:

  • Your samples stay in your browser tab. Training happens on your own computer, "without sending anything to any servers."
  • Closing the tab erases everything. If you close the tab without saving, nothing is kept, in your browser or anywhere else.
  • Two buttons change that. Save project to Drive puts a copy of your samples in your Google Drive. Upload my model (in Export Model) publishes the trained model, but not your samples, at a link anyone who has it can use.

So the camera itself is not the privacy risk. What ends up in the pictures is. A few habits for this course:

  • Record against a plain wall or desk. Check the background for mail with your address, family photos, or a screen with messages on it.
  • Don't record other people without asking them first, and never record people who don't know they're being recorded.
  • Never click Upload my model in this course. Nothing here needs a public link.

Module 6 goes much further into privacy and consent. For now, those three habits cover everything you'll do.

#What to expect from this course

You won't write code here. You'll train real models in Teachable Machine, read charts that show how models behave, and work through thinking exercises that build judgement: is this even a machine learning problem, what will this model actually learn, can I trust this score? The questions get harder, but the tools stay this simple.

There's also an optional extra, Google Colab, for anyone curious about the Python behind the charts. Lesson 3 of this module shows how to open it. Nothing in the course requires it.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You train a model on twenty photos of your room, then close the tab without saving anything. What happened to the photos?

  • Teachable Machine only sends samples anywhere if you save to Drive. Training happens in the tab.

  • The FAQ says that if you close the tab without saving, nothing is saved in your browser or on any servers.

  • Browser history records which pages you visited, not the pictures a page held in memory.

Show answer

B. The FAQ says that if you close the tab without saving, nothing is saved in your browser or on any servers.

2Your friend's camera works on video calls but Teachable Machine shows "There was an error opening your webcam." Which fix should they try first?

  • That's slow and rarely needed. Something simpler is usually holding the camera.

  • The model type doesn't change camera access at all.

  • A camera can usually be used by one app at a time, and call apps often keep it even when minimized.

Show answer

C. A camera can usually be used by one app at a time, and call apps often keep it even when minimized.

3Which of these would put your work on the internet?

  • Training runs inside your browser tab without sending anything to a server.

  • This publishes the trained model at a shareable link. Your samples stay private, but the model is public to anyone with the link.

  • Class names live in the tab with everything else.

Show answer

B. This publishes the trained model at a shareable link. Your samples stay private, but the model is public to anyone with the link.

Key takeaways

  • Teachable Machine runs in Chrome or Firefox with no account, install, or cost.
  • A project has three panels: Classes (your examples), Training, and Preview.
  • A blocked camera is fixed in two places: the browser's site settings and the computer's privacy settings.
  • Samples stay in your tab unless you save to Drive; closing the tab without saving erases them.
  • Check what's in the background before you record.

#Further reading

  • Teachable Machine FAQ (opens in a new tab): Google's answers on privacy, saving, and why models misbehave, in plain language. The "Saving & Exporting" section is the one to read now.
  • Use your camera and microphone in Chrome (opens in a new tab): Google's help page for allowing or blocking sites, if your settings look different from the steps above.
  • Manage your camera and microphone settings on a Chromebook (opens in a new tab): the official guide to ChromeOS privacy controls.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Record examples for two classes using Hold to Record or uploaded photos.
  • Train a model and read the Output bars in Preview.
  • Test the model on new situations and predict the result before you look.
  • Explain why a two-class model still picks a class when you show it nothing.
  • Fix the problems that stop a first training run.

Here's the plan for the next ten minutes. You'll show your webcam about a hundred pictures of your hand, half giving a thumbs-up and half a thumbs-down. You'll click one button. Then you'll hold up your hand and watch a bar jump to "Thumbs up" in real time.

After that comes the part most tutorials skip: trying to break it. A model that works on the pictures you just took proves very little. A model that works on situations you didn't record is the real test, and the very first one you try will probably surprise you.

#Step 1: Name your two classes

Open a new Image Project with the Standard image model, as in the last lesson.

  1. Click the pencil next to Class 1 and type Thumbs up.
  2. Click the pencil next to Class 2 and type Thumbs down.

Names matter more than they seem. The model never reads them; it only sees pictures. But the names are your promise about what each pile should contain, and later you'll check the model against that promise.

#Step 2: Record your examples

On the Thumbs up card, click Webcam. Make a thumbs-up and press and hold Hold to Record. While holding, move: bring your hand closer and farther, tilt it, slide it left and right. Let go after three or four seconds. The card now says something like "84 Image Samples", with thumbnails beside the camera view.

Now do the same on the Thumbs down card, from the same seat, with roughly the same number of samples.

Why all the moving? Every thumbnail is one example. If every example shows your hand in exactly the same spot, the model learns "a hand in that spot". If the examples vary, the only thing they all share is the thing you care about: the direction of the thumb.

💡 Tip

No webcam, or the camera is blocked? Take 30 photos of each gesture on a phone, copy them to your computer, and on each card click Upload, then "Choose images from your files, or drag & drop here." Teachable Machine crops every image to a square, so keep your hand near the middle of the shot.

#Step 3: Train

Click Train Model. You'll see "Preparing training data...", then the button changes to "Training..." with a counter. A message appears: Don't switch tabs! It means it: the browser slows down tabs you aren't looking at, and training can stall. On most laptops this takes under a minute; an older Chromebook can take a few.

When the button reads Model Trained, you're done.

#Step 4: Read the Preview

The Preview panel now shows your webcam with Input switched on, and an Output section with one bar per class. Hold up a thumbs-up. You should see something like this:

Flip your thumb down and the bars swap. That's a working machine learning model, trained by you, running on your computer.

The percentages add up to 100. They show how strongly the model leans toward each class for the picture it's seeing right now. They are not a promise that it's right; Module 5 spends a whole lesson on why a model can be 99% sure and wrong.

#Step 5: Prove it works on things it hasn't seen

Before each test, write down your prediction: which bar will win, and roughly how high? Then try it.

Test Your prediction What happened
Thumbs-up with your other hand
Thumbs-up in a corner of the frame
Thumbs-up with the lights dimmed
A thumbs-sideways
Nothing at all: move out of the frame

The last row is the one to think hardest about. Take your hand away, so the camera sees only the wall behind you.

The model still picks a class. Often with high confidence.

That's not a bug in Teachable Machine; it's how this kind of model works. You gave it exactly two answers to choose from, so it must choose one. It has no idea "neither" is an option, because you never showed it what "neither" looks like. A thumbs-sideways gets forced into one of the two piles the same way.

#Step 6: Teach it "nothing"

  1. Click Add a class and name the new card Nothing.
  2. Click Webcam, step out of the frame, and hold to record the empty background for about the same number of samples as the other classes. Move the camera slightly, or turn a lamp on and off, so the empty scene varies.
  3. Click Train Model again.

Repeat the empty-frame test. Now the Nothing bar should win. You changed nothing about the model's settings, you only changed the examples, and the model's behavior changed with them. That idea, the examples decide what the model learns, runs through this entire course.

#When something goes wrong

⚠️ Watch out

A card says "Class 2" requires at least 1 sample. Training needs at least two classes, and every class that's switched on needs samples. Record into the empty card, or remove it: the three-dot menu on a class card has Delete Class and Disable Class.

⚠️ Watch out

Training seems frozen. You probably switched tabs or minimized the window. Come back to the tab and wait. If it's still stuck after a few minutes, close other tabs (especially video sites), reload, and train again. Your samples are lost on reload unless you saved, so keep the class sizes small (50 to 100 each) on slow computers.

⚠️ Watch out

It always says the same class, whatever you do. Look at your samples. Usually one class has far more examples than the other, or the two classes were recorded in different places, so the model learned the background instead of your hand. Record both classes from the same seat with similar numbers of samples, then retrain.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You trained Thumbs up and Thumbs down only. You point the camera at an empty chair and see "Thumbs down 91%". What's the best explanation?

  • The model isn't reasoning about shapes like you do. It has to pick from the two answers it knows.

  • With no "Nothing" class, every picture gets forced into Thumbs up or Thumbs down, often with high confidence.

  • Training worked; the model is doing exactly what two classes allow. The fix is a new class, not a rerun.

Show answer

B. With no "Nothing" class, every picture gets forced into Thumbs up or Thumbs down, often with high confidence.

2Your thumbs-up samples were recorded in your bedroom and your thumbs-down samples in the kitchen. The model scores perfectly in each room. What has it most likely learned?

  • It might have, but you can't tell, because the room alone separates the two classes.

  • Background is the biggest, easiest difference between the two piles, so the model can lean on it. Test with a thumbs-down in the bedroom to find out.

  • The model sees the whole picture. Nothing tells it to ignore the background.

Show answer

B. Background is the biggest, easiest difference between the two piles, so the model can lean on it. Test with a thumbs-down in the bedroom to find out.

3What changed the model's behavior when you added the Nothing class?

  • You didn't touch Advanced; the settings were identical.

  • New examples gave the model a third answer and showed it what that answer looks like.

  • Nothing outside your tab changed between the two training runs.

Show answer

B. New examples gave the model a third answer and showed it what that answer looks like.

Key takeaways

  • The workflow is gather, train, test on new things, then change the examples if it's wrong.
  • Varied examples teach the thing you care about; identical examples teach the spot, the light, or the background.
  • The Output bars show how strongly the model leans, not whether it's right.
  • A model can only answer with the classes it was given, so "nothing" needs its own class.
  • Keep the tab in front of you while training.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Save a project as a .tm file or to Google Drive, and open it again.
  • Organize your course files so you can find any project later.
  • Keep a model journal that records what you changed, what you predicted, and what happened.
  • Work through the common camera, training, and prediction problems in a fixed order.
  • Open Google Colab and run a cell (optional).

Teachable Machine keeps everything in the open tab. That's why it's private, and it's also why the most common way to lose an hour of work is a single click on the wrong ×. If you try to leave with unsaved samples, the page warns you: "You have unsaved data. Are you sure you'd like to exit?" Believe it.

This lesson sets up three habits that make the rest of the course smoother: save every project, write down every experiment, and debug in a fixed order instead of clicking around.

#Save a project two ways

Everything lives in the menu: click the button with three lines at the top left of a project page.

Download a file (no account)

  1. Open the menu and choose Download project as file.
  2. Your browser saves a file ending in .tm to your Downloads folder. It holds every class and every sample.
  3. To pick up where you left off, open Teachable Machine, open the menu, and choose Open project from file. Pick the .tm file.

This is the right choice on a shared or school computer: you can carry the file on a USB stick, and nothing goes to any online account.

Save to Google Drive

  1. Open the menu and choose Save project to Drive.
  2. The first time, it asks you to log in to Google Drive. Then it asks you to Name your project.
  3. To reopen, choose Open project from Drive from the menu, or from the New Project screen.
  4. After you change anything, save again. Drive keeps the version you last saved, not the one on your screen.

Drive saves are handy across computers, but they need a Google account (see the note on accounts below).

You can also save just one class's examples. On a class card, the three-dot menu has Download Samples, which makes a zip of that class's pictures. It's handy for keeping a set of test pictures apart from your training samples.

📝 Note

Downloading a project file is different from Export Model. A project file keeps your samples so you can keep training. Export Model makes a finished model for use in websites and apps, and it isn't needed anywhere in this course.

#Name files so future-you can find them

Make one folder for the course and one subfolder per module. Name each project with the module, the idea, and a version number:

The version number is the important part. When an experiment makes things worse, you want the earlier version back, and final-final-2.tm won't tell you which one that was.

#Keep a model journal

Machine learning is mostly experiments: change one thing, retrain, test, compare. Without notes you'll forget which change helped, and after three rounds everything blurs together. Use a notebook, a document, or a spreadsheet, with one row per experiment:

Date Project What I changed My prediction What happened Why I think so
Oct 3 m1-thumbs-v1 Nothing: first model Works on both hands Right hand fine, left hand 50/50 Every sample was my right hand
Oct 3 m1-thumbs-v2 Added a Nothing class, 60 samples Empty room → Nothing Nothing wins at 95% It finally has a third answer

Two columns do most of the work. My prediction forces you to commit before you look, which is how you find out whether your mental picture of the model is right. Why I think so turns a surprise into a lesson.

The journal also catches lopsided classes. Here's a chart of the sample counts from a project where one class got far fewer examples than the others:

A model trained on this has seen four times as many hands as empty rooms. When it's unsure, it will tend to guess a hand. If your journal shows counts like these, record more samples for the short class before blaming anything else.

#Get unstuck in a fixed order

When something breaks, work down this chart instead of trying random fixes:

Symptom Most likely cause Fix
"Could not open your camera. You may have denied access." You clicked Block Allow the site in browser settings, then reload
Black camera view Another app holds the camera Quit call apps completely, reload
Training never finishes Tab was hidden or the computer is slow Keep the tab in front; train with 50 to 100 samples per class
One class always wins Unequal sample counts, or classes recorded in different places Balance the counts; record all classes in the same spot
Perfect at your desk, wrong elsewhere Examples were all from one spot Add samples from other places and lighting

Notice that the last three rows aren't fixed in the settings. They're fixed in the examples. That's the most common surprise for beginners, and it's the subject of Module 3.

When you ask someone for help, give them four things: what you did, what you expected, what happened, and a screenshot. Check the screenshot first; crop out other people and anything personal in the background.

#Optional: open Google Colab

Google Colab runs Python notebooks on Google's computers, in the browser, for free. Every chart in this course is drawn by a short Python program, and if you're curious, you can paste one into Colab and change the numbers. You'll never need it to complete a lesson.

  1. Go to colab.research.google.com and sign in with a Google account.
  2. Create a new notebook. Depending on the version, it's a New notebook button in the opening window or File › New notebook in Drive.
  3. Click inside the empty code cell and paste the chart program from above.
  4. Press Shift + Enter, or click the round play button at the left of the cell. The chart appears under the cell.

Change 20 to 80 in the program and run it again: the bars even out.

⚠️ Watch out

Colab asks you to sign in, or won't open at all. Colab needs a Google account. Google requires you to be at least 13 (the age differs in some countries) to manage your own account; younger learners need a parent-managed account through Family Link. School Google accounts sometimes have Colab switched off by the school. All of this is fine to skip: Colab is a bonus, not a requirement.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1You'll finish a project tomorrow on a different school computer, and you don't have a Google account. What should you do before closing the tab?

  • The file holds every class and sample, and Open project from file restores it on any computer.

  • An exported model can't be trained further in Teachable Machine; it doesn't keep your samples.

  • The bookmark only saves the address. The samples vanish when the tab closes.

Show answer

A. The file holds every class and sample, and Open project from file restores it on any computer.

2Your model works at your desk but fails in the kitchen. Which journal entry would help you most next time?

  • This records that something failed, but not what you changed or why.

  • It records the change, the prediction, the result, and a reason you can act on: add samples from other places.

  • Without the conditions and your prediction, you can't learn anything from it later.

Show answer

B. It records the change, the prediction, the result, and a reason you can act on: add samples from other places.

Key takeaways

  • Save with Download project as file (a .tm file) or Save project to Drive; closing the tab without saving loses everything.
  • Name projects with the module, the idea, and a version number.
  • A journal row records the change, your prediction, the result, and why.
  • Debug in order: camera, then training, then predictions. Most prediction problems are fixed by changing the examples.
  • Colab is optional; it lets you rerun the course's charts if you're curious.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Decide whether a system follows rules a person wrote or patterns it learned from examples.
  • Explain how AI, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI fit inside each other.
  • Name the task family of a system (classification, regression, clustering, recommendation, or generation) from the kind of answer it gives.
  • Describe what a chatbot is actually doing when it answers, and what that means for trusting it.

A school newsletter announces five "AI-powered" upgrades:

  1. The bell rings automatically at 8:05.
  2. The email system moves spam to a junk folder.
  3. The attendance system emails a parent after three absences.
  4. The library website says "students who borrowed this also borrowed…"
  5. A help-desk chatbot answers questions about the timetable.

Two of these involve no learning at all. Someone wrote the bell time and the "three absences" rule down, and the computer follows them exactly. The other three were shaped by examples. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to sort any system like this in about ten seconds, and say what kind of task it's doing.

#Rules: a person wrote the decision down

A rule-based system follows instructions someone typed in: if absences ≥ 3, email the parent. Rules are predictable, easy to explain, and easy to change. Ask "why did it email my mom?" and the answer is one sentence.

Rules break in a specific way: on cases the writer didn't imagine. Try writing rules for spam. "If the email contains FREE, it's spam" catches some spam, but also your friend's message about free pizza at the club meeting. Add an exception, then another, and soon you have hundreds of rules that still miss spam written in new ways.

#Machine learning: the decision is learned from examples

Machine learning flips the job around. Instead of writing the rule, you collect examples where the right answer is already known (thousands of emails people marked as spam or not spam) and a training process finds the pattern for you. The result is a model: something that takes a new email and returns an answer.

That's exactly what you did with thumbs up and thumbs down. You never described what a thumbs-up looks like. You gave labeled pictures, and training worked out the pattern.

The test for "is this machine learning?" is one question: who wrote the decision, a person or a training process? It's not whether the system uses data (the attendance rule uses data), and it's not whether the company calls it AI.

#AI is the umbrella; machine learning is one way to get there

Artificial intelligence is the broadest term: any system that does something we'd normally say takes intelligence, like playing chess, recognizing speech, or planning a route. Older AI was often built mostly from rules. IBM's Deep Blue, which beat the world chess champion in 1997, searched through millions of moves using scoring rules written with help from chess experts.

  • Machine learning is the part of AI where behavior is learned from examples.
  • Deep learning is machine learning with neural networks that have many layers. Module 4 shows how one learns. The model inside Teachable Machine is one.
  • Generative AI is deep learning used to produce new text, images, audio, or video, like chatbots and image generators.

So every chatbot is deep learning, which is machine learning, which is AI. But not all AI is machine learning, and plenty of things labeled "AI" in advertising are plain rules.

#Five task families, told apart by the answer

Once you know a system learned from data, the next question is: what kind of answer does it give? That decides almost everything else, including what data it needs and how you'd check it.

Task family The answer is… Everyday examples
Classification one label from a fixed list spam or not spam; which bird is at the feeder; thumbs up or down
Regression a number on a scale minutes until the bus arrives; tomorrow's high temperature; a house price
Clustering groups that nobody labeled in advance a photo app grouping faces; a store grouping shoppers by habits
Recommendation a ranked list chosen for one person the next video; songs "for you"; "also borrowed" at the library
Generation something new: text, an image, a sound a chatbot's reply; an image from a prompt; autocomplete

Three of these are easiest to tell apart in a picture. Each dot below is one example:

Left, classification. Every email arrives already labeled, and the model's job is to draw a dividing line (the dashed one) so a new email can be put on the right side. The answer is a category.

Middle, regression. The answer is a number that can land anywhere on a scale. The model draws a trend line, and a new delivery 5 km away gets the time on the line above 5.

Right, clustering. Nobody labeled these shoppers. The colors were found by an algorithm that grouped dots close to each other. A store might then notice "the frequent small spenders" and treat them differently. Nobody told it those groups existed.

A quick way to separate the first two: ask whether an answer halfway between two others makes sense. Halfway between 20 and 30 minutes is 25 minutes, so delivery time is regression. Halfway between "spam" and "not spam" isn't a thing, so that's classification.

#What a chatbot is actually doing

A chatbot like ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude is built on a large language model. It was trained on an enormous amount of text to do one thing: given some text, predict what comes next, one small piece at a time. It was then trained further, with people rating its answers, to follow instructions and be helpful. That makes it a generation system.

That one fact explains most of its behavior:

  • It writes what is likely, not what is checked. Fluent, confident text is what it's built to produce, whether or not the facts are right. Made-up book titles, quotes, and citations are a well-known result.
  • Its knowledge stops at its training data. Some chatbot apps add tools like web search. Then the model can read current pages, but it still writes the answer by predicting text, so it can misread or misquote them.
  • It isn't looking answers up in a database, and sounding sure doesn't mean it is sure. Module 5 is about exactly this gap.

Chatbots are very good at drafting, explaining, rephrasing, and brainstorming. They're risky when you need a fact to be true and don't check it.

⚠️ Watch out

"It uses data, so it's machine learning." Rules use data too: the attendance system reads absence counts. The question is whether the decision was written by a person or learned from examples.

⚠️ Watch out

"The answer is a number, so it's regression." Numbers can be names. A zip code or a jersey number is a label: halfway between zip 94110 and 94112 isn't a place. Use the halfway test, not the digits.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Thermostat A turns the heat on whenever the room drops below 19°C. Thermostat B notices when you turn the heat up each day and starts doing it for you. Which one uses machine learning?

  • Measuring something is data, but the 19°C rule was written by a person.

  • Nobody typed in your schedule; it was learned from examples of what you did.

  • Automatic isn't the same as learned. A light timer is automatic too.

Show answer

B. Nobody typed in your schedule; it was learned from examples of what you did.

2A music app shows a list of 20 songs "picked for you", best match first. Which task family is that?

  • It isn't putting each song into one of a few fixed labels.

  • The songs already exist; nothing new is being created.

  • It ranks existing items for one particular person. That's the shape of a recommendation answer.

Show answer

C. It ranks existing items for one particular person. That's the shape of a recommendation answer.

3Which of these is a regression task?

  • Two possible answers from a fixed list is classification.

  • The answer is a number on a scale, and halfway between 4 and 6 minutes (5 minutes) makes sense.

  • Route numbers are names. Halfway between route 12 and route 14 is not route 13.

Show answer

B. The answer is a number on a scale, and halfway between 4 and 6 minutes (5 minutes) makes sense.

4A chatbot gives you a perfect-sounding quote and the book it came from for your essay. What's the sensible next step?

  • Training on text doesn't mean it retrieves exact quotes. It predicts likely text, which can include invented quotes.

  • A generation system produces plausible text. Checking the source is the only way to know it's real.

  • Its answer to that is also predicted text. Confidence in its reply doesn't verify anything.

Show answer

B. A generation system produces plausible text. Checking the source is the only way to know it's real.

Key takeaways

  • Rule-based systems follow decisions a person wrote; machine learning systems learn decisions from examples with known answers.
  • AI contains machine learning, which contains deep learning, which contains generative AI.
  • Name the task by its answer: a label (classification), a number (regression), unlabeled groups (clustering), a ranked list for one person (recommendation), or something new (generation).
  • The halfway test separates regression from classification.
  • Chatbots generate likely text; that's why they're fluent, and why their facts need checking.

#Further reading

  • What is Machine Learning? (Google for Developers) (opens in a new tab): a short, clear page on the main types of machine learning, from Google's machine learning courses.
  • Elements of AI, Chapter 1 (opens in a new tab): a free course from the University of Helsinki that's excellent on what does and doesn't count as AI.
  • How AI Works (Code.org) (opens in a new tab): the full video series, including the chatbot episode above.

What you'll learn

  • Write a rule-based clap detector and predict where it fails.
  • Train a three-class Teachable Machine audio model: Background Noise, Clap, and Snap.
  • Test the model with sounds it never heard and record what it does.
  • Name the model's task family and explain how a different question would change it.
  • Explain why the learned model can separate sounds that a loudness rule can't.

You're going to build the same thing twice. First as a rule, the way a programmer would have done it before machine learning: "if the sound is loud enough, it's a clap." Then as a model trained on your own claps and snaps in Teachable Machine.

Here's the finished model, listening:

Then you'll throw sounds at both versions that neither was built for, and see which one copes.

#Step 1: Write the rule first

On paper, finish this rule: "If the sound is louder than ___, it's a clap."

Now predict: which other sounds would also pass your rule? Think about a book dropping, a cough, a door closing, a knock on the desk.

Here's how one set of sounds measured on a 0 to 100 loudness scale. These are example numbers; your room would give different ones, but the pattern is the same:

Every bar above the orange line counts as a clap under the rule. The knock, the cough, and the door all pass, so the rule has three false alarms out of four alarms. Raise the line above 82 to stop them and you'd miss the clap too, while the door still gets through.

A single loudness number just doesn't carry enough information to separate these sounds. Keep that thought for Step 7.

#Step 2: Start an Audio Project and allow the microphone

  1. Go to teachablemachine.withgoogle.com, click Get Started, then Audio Project.
  2. The first card is already named Background Noise. Its note says an audio model needs at least 20 seconds of background noise, and that this class can't be deleted or disabled.
  3. Click Mic on that card. Your browser asks to use the microphone; allow it, exactly as you allowed the camera in Module 1. If you see "There was an error opening your microphone," the fixes are the same as for the camera, in the browser's site settings and the computer's privacy settings.

#Step 3: Record the background

Click Record 20 Seconds and stay quiet. Don't hold your breath or turn everything off; record the room as it normally sounds, fan and traffic included. When it finishes, click Extract Sample. The card fills with twenty one-second samples, each shown as a small spectrogram: time runs left to right, pitch runs bottom to top, and brighter means louder.

Why does Teachable Machine insist on this class? Because a sound model is listening all the time. Most of what it hears is nothing in particular. Without a Background Noise class, every quiet second would be forced into Clap or Snap, just like the empty room in your thumbs model.

#Step 4: Record the Clap class

  1. Rename Class 2 to Clap with the pencil icon.
  2. Click Mic. The button reads Record 2 Seconds. Click it and clap once or twice inside the two seconds.
  3. Click Extract Sample. Each second becomes one sample.
  4. Repeat until the card shows at least 8 samples (it marks the minimum), and aim for about 20.

Vary them: some loud, some soft, some close to the microphone and some from arm's length, one hand cupped and then flat. A one-second sample with no clap in it teaches the wrong thing, so check them: click a sample to open it larger, where you can play it back and delete it.

#Step 5: Record the Snap class

Click Add a class, name it Snap, and record about 20 samples of finger snaps the same way. Can't snap? Use Whistle or Tap (tapping a pen on the desk) instead. Anything works, as long as it's a sound you can make on purpose many times.

#Step 6: Train it and test it like a skeptic

Click Train Model and keep the tab in front of you. When it's done, the Preview starts listening and the Output bars move as you make sounds.

Before each test, write your prediction in your journal. Then try it:

Sound you make You predict Top bar
A clap Clap
A snap Snap
Saying the word "clap"
A knock on the desk
A cough
Clapping from across the room

The first two should work. The interesting rows are the others, especially the knock and the cough. The model has three answers and must pick one, so a sound it never heard goes to whichever class it most resembles. A knock often lands in Clap. Saying "clap" usually doesn't, because the word sounds nothing like the noise.

Clapping from across the room tests something else: whether your samples covered distance. If it fails, you know which samples to add.

#Step 7: Why the model beats the rule

The model got a knock right that the rule got wrong. Here's why. The rule used one number: loudness. The model looks at the whole spectrogram, including how much of the sound sits in high pitches and how fast it fades. Plot just two measurements per sound and the difference shows:

Read it left to right first, the way the rule does. Claps, snaps, and knocks all spread across the dashed line, so no vertical line can split them. Now read it bottom to top. Knocks sit low (mostly low-pitched thuds), claps in the middle, snaps high. With two measurements, the groups barely overlap.

The real model uses far more than two measurements: every pitch band at every moment of the clip. And nobody had to choose them. Training found which patterns separate your classes. That's the advantage of learning from examples, and the reason it needed examples of every sound it should know.

#The finished project

Save it with Download project as file.

#Same goal, different task

The model is a classifier: it picks one label from a fixed list. Change the question, and the task family changes with it:

  • "How many claps were in the last ten seconds?" needs a count, a number: closer to regression.
  • "Make a clapping rhythm that fits this song" needs something new: generation.
  • "Which clapping games would this kid like?" needs a ranked list for one person: recommendation.

The microphone and the sounds are the same in all four. What you want back decides the task.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does Teachable Machine require a Background Noise class in every audio project?

  • It isn't a calibration step. It's a class like any other.

  • The model listens constantly, and most seconds contain no clap or snap. Without this class, silence would always be labeled as one of them.

  • Two classes can train fine. The requirement is about what the model hears between your sounds.

Show answer

B. The model listens constantly, and most seconds contain no clap or snap. Without this class, silence would always be labeled as one of them.

2You recorded every clap with your hands right next to the laptop. What should you expect when you clap from across the room?

  • To the model, a distant clap is quieter and echoier. It only knows the claps you showed it.

  • The fix is to add clap samples recorded from farther away.

  • More echo makes it less like your training samples, not more.

Show answer

B. The fix is to add clap samples recorded from farther away.

3A dog barks and the Clap bar jumps to 80%. What's the most sensible fix?

  • Volume won't give the model a correct answer to choose for a bark.

  • More training on the same three classes still leaves no class for barks.

  • The model can only answer with the classes it has. Giving it an "other" answer, with varied examples, is the fix.

Show answer

C. The model can only answer with the classes it has. Giving it an "other" answer, with varied examples, is the fix.

Key takeaways

  • A loudness rule fails because one number can't separate sounds that differ in pitch and shape.
  • A trained sound model looks at the whole spectrogram and finds the patterns that separate your classes.
  • Background Noise gives the model an answer for "nothing happening".
  • Sounds the model never heard are forced into the closest class, so test with them on purpose.
  • The task family comes from the answer you want: the same sounds can feed classification, regression, generation, or recommendation.

#Extend it

  • Add an Other sounds class with knocks, coughs, and talking, retrain, and repeat the Step 6 tests.
  • Ask someone else to clap and snap (with their permission). Does it work for them? Teachable Machine's FAQ suggests exactly this test.
  • Make a rule and a model work together: only count a clap if the Clap bar is above 90%. Is that better or worse?

#Further reading

  • Teachable Machine FAQ: "Why isn't it working like I want it to?" (opens in a new tab): ideas for breaking your model on purpose, including changing microphones and rooms.
  • Speech Command Recognizer (TensorFlow.js) (opens in a new tab): the pre-trained sound model Teachable Machine builds on. The README explains how it turns audio into spectrograms; skim the overview, skip the code.

m2-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Decide quickly whether a system's decisions were written by people or learned from examples.
  • Name the task family of everyday AI products from the shape of their answers.
  • Turn one real-world goal into classification, regression, clustering, and recommendation versions.
  • Judge common claims about chatbots using what you know about how they generate text.
  • Argue when a plain rule is a better choice than machine learning.

These exercises are for thinking, not typing. Write your answers in your journal before opening a solution; the point is to find out where your picture of AI is fuzzy, and you can't do that if you peek.

Keep this flowchart open. It's the question order that works for almost any system:

#Warm-up

For each answer, say whether it's a label, a number, or a ranked list: "Rain" / "73%" / "5 videos, best first" / "Golden retriever" / "$212,000".

Show solution

"Rain" is a label. "73%" is a number (though it could be a confidence attached to a label; Module 5 untangles that). "5 videos, best first" is a ranked list. "Golden retriever" is a label. "$212,000" is a number.

#Exercise 1: Rule or learned?

Decide whether each system's key decision was most likely written by a person or learned from examples. Give a one-line reason.

  1. A microwave's "Popcorn" button runs for 2 minutes 30 seconds.
  2. A phone unlocks when it sees your face.
  3. The library charges 25 cents per day for late books.
  4. A photo app groups your pictures by which person is in them.
  5. A traffic light changes every 45 seconds.
  6. An email service moves messages to the junk folder.
Need a hint?

Ask: could you write the decision as one or two sentences that cover every case? If yes, someone probably did.

Show solution
  1. Rule. A fixed time someone chose.
  2. Learned. Nobody can write rules for every face, angle, and lighting condition; face recognition is trained on examples.
  3. Rule. A formula: days late × $0.25.
  4. Learned, and specifically clustering. Nobody labeled your photos; the app groups faces that look alike, and you add names afterward.
  5. Rule. A timer. (Some cities use sensors and smarter timing, but a fixed 45 seconds is a rule.)
  6. Learned, usually with some rules added. Spam filters learn from millions of messages people mark as spam, and many also have hand-written rules, like blocking known scam senders. Real systems often mix both.

#Exercise 2: Name the task family

Name the task family for each product.

  1. A weather app shows tomorrow's high: 18°C.
  2. A plant-identifying app says "Monstera deliciosa".
  3. A streaming service's "Because you watched…" row.
  4. An app that turns your sketch into a finished-looking painting.
  5. A bank flags a card payment as "possible fraud".
  6. A school groups 400 students' survey answers into "types" of study habits, without deciding the types in advance.
  7. A map app estimates you'll arrive at 4:52 p.m.
  8. A keyboard suggests the next word as you type.
Need a hint?

Look only at the output. Is it one label from a list, a number on a scale, a ranked list for you, groups nobody named, or something that didn't exist before?

Show solution
  1. Regression: a temperature is a number, and 18.5°C makes sense.
  2. Classification: one species from a fixed list.
  3. Recommendation: a ranked list chosen for you.
  4. Generation: a new image.
  5. Classification: fraud or not fraud.
  6. Clustering: the groups are found, not given.
  7. Regression: an arrival time is a number on a scale (minutes from now).
  8. Generation, and also a little like classification: it picks likely next words from a vocabulary. This is the same next-word prediction that sits inside chatbots, just much smaller.

#Exercise 3: One goal, four framings

A school cafeteria throws away too much food. Write one machine learning task for each family that could help: classification, regression, clustering, and recommendation. For each, say what the model's answer would be.

Need a hint?

Start from the answers the cafeteria staff would find useful. "How much?" is a number. "Which kind of day is this?" is a label. "Which students eat alike?" is groups.

Show solution

One good set (yours can differ):

  • Regression: predict how many servings of each dish will be eaten tomorrow. Answer: a number, like 212 servings of pasta.
  • Classification: predict whether tomorrow will be a "low", "normal", or "high" attendance day. Answer: one of three labels.
  • Clustering: group the weekly menus by how much food was wasted, to discover which kinds of menus waste the most. Answer: groups nobody named in advance.
  • Recommendation: suggest to each student the dishes they're most likely to finish. Answer: a ranked list per student.

Notice that the regression version is probably the most useful, and also that a simple rule ("cook what was eaten last Tuesday") might get you most of the way. That's Exercise 6.

#Exercise 4: Number or category?

For each prediction, decide whether it's better treated as classification or regression, and use the halfway test to justify it.

  1. A student's final letter grade (A to F).
  2. The number of minutes a student spends on homework.
  3. A shoe size.
  4. Someone's age, guessed from a photo.
  5. The zip code a package is going to.
Need a hint?

Halfway between two answers: does it mean something? If yes, it's a scale. If not, the "numbers" are names.

Show solution
  1. Classification, though an ordered one. There's no grade halfway between B and C in most schools. (If the school used a 0 to 100 percentage instead, that would be regression.)
  2. Regression. Halfway between 30 and 40 minutes is 35 minutes, which is meaningful.
  3. Either, and it's a real choice. Shoe sizes come in fixed steps (8, 8.5, 9), which looks like classification, but halfway between 8 and 9 is 8.5, a real size. Treating it as regression and rounding works well.
  4. Regression. Halfway between 30 and 40 is 35, a real age.
  5. Classification. Zip 94110 and 94112 aren't "two apart" in any useful way. They're names that happen to be written with digits.

#Exercise 5: Judge the chatbot claims

A friend makes each of these claims. Say whether it's right, wrong, or "it depends", and explain using how chatbots work.

  1. "It told me the library closes at 6, so it does."
  2. "It gave me a citation with an author and a page number, so the article exists."
  3. "It can't possibly know about anything that happened this week."
  4. "It's basically searching a giant database of answers."
  5. "It wrote a great first draft of my speech, so I'll edit that."
Need a hint?

A language model produces text that's likely to come next. Some chatbot apps also give it tools, like web search. Which claims depend on whether a tool was used?

Show solution
  1. Wrong as reasoning. It may be right, but a likely-sounding answer isn't a checked one. Opening hours change, and the model may be repeating old text or inventing a plausible time. Check the library's own website.
  2. Wrong. Invented citations, with real-looking authors and page numbers, are a well-known failure. A citation exists only once you've found it.
  3. It depends. The model's built-in knowledge stops at its training data. If the app searched the web, it can mention this week's news, though it can still misread what it found.
  4. Wrong. There's no lookup table of answers. It generates new text each time, which is why the same question can get different answers.
  5. Right. Drafting is a strength: the task is "produce plausible, well-organized text", which is exactly what the model is trained to do. Your editing supplies the facts and the voice.

#Exercise 6: Should this use machine learning at all?

For each problem, recommend a rule or machine learning, and give the reason.

  1. Calculating a student's final grade from homework (30%), tests (50%), and a project (20%).
  2. Sorting thousands of photos from a school trip into "has the class banner in it" and "doesn't".
  3. Deciding whether a student can borrow another library book (limit: 5 at a time).
  4. Spotting which of 2,000 written survey answers mention bullying, in any wording.
Need a hint?

When the rule is known exactly and must be applied the same way every time, a person can write it, and learning adds only risk.

Show solution
  1. Rule. The formula is known and must be exactly the same for everyone. A learned model could only add mistakes, and nobody could appeal its decision.
  2. Machine learning. "Contains a banner" is easy to recognize and nearly impossible to describe as rules about pixels. A Teachable Machine image model is a reasonable start.
  3. Rule. "Borrowed fewer than 5" is one line.
  4. Machine learning, with people checking. People describe bullying in endless ways, so word lists miss a lot. A model can flag likely answers, but because the stakes are high, a person should read every flagged answer, and some unflagged ones too.

A pattern to keep: machine learning earns its place when the rule is hard to write down. When the rule is easy and fairness depends on it being exact, use the rule.

#Challenge: Design an AI feature for the school library

Propose one feature for a school library that uses machine learning. Write a half-page covering:

  • The task family, and exactly what the model's answer looks like.
  • The examples it would learn from, and where the known answers (labels) come from.
  • The rule-based version someone could build instead, and why yours is better (or isn't).
  • How you'd check it works on books or students it never saw.
  • One way it could go wrong for a particular student.
Need a hint?

Recommendation ("books for you") is the obvious choice. A more surprising one: classification of returned books as "needs repair" from a photo of the spine.

Show solution

An example answer, for a "needs repair" classifier:

  • Task: classification. Answer: "Needs repair" or "OK" for each returned book, from a photo of its spine and cover.
  • Examples: photos of returned books over a term, labeled by the librarian who already decides which go to the repair box. The labels come from that existing human decision.
  • Rule-based alternative: "check books older than 10 years". It's easy but wrong in both directions: old books in good shape get pulled, and a new book with a torn spine is missed. The photo model looks at the actual damage.
  • Checking it: hold back a set of labeled photos from a different month, never used in training, and compare the model's answers with the librarian's. (Module 4 is about doing this properly.)
  • Could go wrong: if almost every training photo was taken under the desk lamp, books photographed in daylight might be misjudged. And if the model is wrong, a student could be blamed for damage they didn't cause, so the librarian should make the final call.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Describe a dataset as rows of examples, columns of features, and one label column.
  • Explain how the choice of features decides what a model can and can't tell apart.
  • Read a decision boundary on a chart and predict what a model says about a new example.
  • Separate training (examples with labels) from inference (new examples, no label).
  • Spot features that leak the answer or won't exist when the model is used.

A recycling plant has a machine that sorts aluminum cans from plastic bottles on a conveyor belt. It doesn't "see" a can the way you do. For each object it measures two numbers: how heavy it is, and how much light bounces off it. That's all it gets. A crushed can and a plastic bottle wrapped in foil look almost the same to it.

Every machine learning model works like this. It never sees the thing itself, only the numbers someone chose to measure about it. Choose well and the job is easy. Choose badly and no amount of training will help.

#Data is a table

Here's what the sorter's training data looks like:

Weight (g) Shininess (0–10) See-through? Label
15 8 no Can
21 3 yes Plastic
14 7 no Can
19 4 yes Plastic
17 6 no Can
16 5 no Plastic

Three words describe every part of it:

  • Example: one row. One object that went past the sensors.
  • Feature: one column the model gets to look at. Weight, shininess, see-through.
  • Label: the column with the right answer, filled in by a person. It's the thing the model is learning to produce.

A model trained on rows like these is doing supervised learning: learning from examples where the answer is supplied. Clustering, from Module 2, is the unsupervised version: the same table with the label column missing.

The label isn't a fixed part of the data; it depends on your question. Give the same table a label column of "recycling value in cents", and you're training a regression model on identical features.

#The features decide what a model can notice

Look at the last row of the table: a dull, 16-gram piece of plastic. On weight alone, it sits right among the cans. Here's what happens across 40 objects when the model gets one feature, and then two:

Left panel. With only weight, the model has a single number line. Cans and bottles overlap between about 13 and 18 grams, so wherever you put a cut-off, many objects land on the wrong side. This is the loudness rule from the clap detector all over again.

Right panel. Add shininess and the two groups pull apart: cans high, bottles low. The model learned the gray line, called the decision boundary. Everything in the blue region gets called a can, everything in the orange region plastic. A new object is placed on this chart by its two measurements, and the color under it is the prediction.

Two things to notice. First, one can lands on the wrong side (a dull, dented one near weight 17, shininess 5). Even good features leave some overlap, which is why the printout says 98%, not 100%. Second, the model never chose to look at shininess. We chose to measure it. Picking features is a human decision, and it often matters more than anything the model does afterward.

#Training versus inference

A model has two separate lives, and keeping them apart clears up most confusion about how machine learning works:

Training uses the full table, labels included, to produce the model. Inference is using the model: a new object arrives, its features are measured, and the model supplies the label. There's no label at inference time; if there were, you wouldn't need a model.

That leads to a rule worth memorizing: every feature must be available at the moment of prediction. A feature measured after the fact is useless, however well it predicts during training.

#Pictures and sounds are tables too

When you trained the thumbs model, where were the features? Every image is already a table of numbers. Here's an 8×8 scan of a handwritten digit that ships with the scikit-learn library, printed as numbers and then drawn:

You can see the zero in the numbers if you squint: a ring of high values around a middle of zeros. This one image is one row of a table with 64 feature columns, and its label is 0.

Teachable Machine's photos are 224×224 pixels in color, which is 224 × 224 × 3 = 150,528 numbers per example. Raw pixels make poor features, though: move your hand two centimeters and almost every number changes. So Teachable Machine first runs each picture through a network Google already trained on a huge collection of photos (it's called MobileNet), which turns the pixels into a much shorter list of more useful features, things closer to "edges here, a round shape there". Your classes are learned on top of those. This trick is called transfer learning, and it's why your model trained in under a minute on a hundred photos.

The consequence is important for the next lesson: in Teachable Machine you don't choose features. You only choose examples. Examples are your one steering wheel.

#Labels come from people, and people disagree

Somebody filled in the label column. Is a juice box paper or plastic? Is a can with a plastic label a can? If two people labeled the same objects differently, the model learns a blur of both opinions. Teams that label data write a labeling rule first ("anything with a metal body is a Can, whatever its label") and check that labelers agree. Module 5 returns to what happens when the people or examples behind a dataset are lopsided.

⚠️ Watch out

A feature that secretly contains the label. Suppose the sorter's table had a column "which bin a worker put it in". It would predict perfectly in training, because it is the label written another way. At inference time there's no worker, so the column doesn't exist. If a feature seems too good to be true, ask whether it's the answer in disguise. This is called leakage.

⚠️ Watch out

Features that look like numbers but carry no meaning. A student ID or a row number is a number, but a model will happily find patterns in it (maybe IDs assigned later belong to younger students). That pattern won't hold for new data. Only use features that plausibly relate to the answer.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A model predicts whether a student will pass a course, using a table with columns: hours of sleep, homework done (%), attendance (%), and final exam score. What's wrong with this setup if predictions are needed in week 3?

  • It is a number, and it could plausibly matter.

  • Every feature must be available when the prediction is made. This one leaks the label and arrives too late.

  • Four features can be plenty. The problem is which ones, not how many.

Show answer

B. Every feature must be available when the prediction is made. This one leaks the label and arrives too late.

2On the right-hand chart, a new object weighs 24 g and has a shininess of 9. What does the model predict?

  • Weight alone would suggest that, but the model uses both features. At shininess 9 it's above the line.

  • Find 24 on the weight axis and 9 on the shininess axis: the region there is blue.

  • A model always predicts; the boundary covers every point. Whether to trust a prediction far from the training data is a separate question.

Show answer

B. Find 24 on the weight axis and 9 on the shininess axis: the region there is blue.

3Same objects, same sensors, but now the label column is "recycling value in cents". What changed?

  • The features are identical. Changing the question changes the label, and the label decides the task.

  • The features are the same, but the model is now learning to produce a different kind of answer.

  • There's still a label column filled in by people, so it's still supervised.

Show answer

A. The features are identical. Changing the question changes the label, and the label decides the task.

4In Teachable Machine, what's the main way you control which features your model relies on?

  • Teachable Machine doesn't let you choose features. A pre-trained network computes them from each picture.

  • The model leans on whatever reliably differs between your classes, so varied examples steer it toward what you care about.

  • The model never reads class names.

Show answer

B. The model leans on whatever reliably differs between your classes, so varied examples steer it toward what you care about.

Key takeaways

  • A dataset is a table: each row is an example, the columns are features, and the label is the answer a person supplied.
  • The features decide what a model can tell apart; picking them is a human choice that often matters most.
  • A decision boundary divides the feature space; a new example gets the label of the region it lands in.
  • Training uses features and labels; inference sees features only, so every feature must exist at prediction time.
  • Images are tables of numbers too. Teachable Machine computes features for you, so your examples are how you steer it.

#Further reading

  • Supervised Learning (Google for Developers) (opens in a new tab): Google's own explanation of features, labels, training, and inference, with a rain-prediction example.
  • Teachable Machine FAQ: "What's happening on the machine learning side?" (opens in a new tab): the short official description of transfer learning in Teachable Machine.

m3-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Plan a dataset on paper: classes, a labeling rule, and a secret test set.
  • Train a three-class image model and test it on objects it has never seen.
  • Improve a model by changing only its examples, with every setting left the same.
  • Design an experiment that reveals a shortcut the model learned instead of the real idea.

In the last lesson the recycling sorter got to measure weight and shininess. Teachable Machine doesn't let you pick features: a pre-trained network computes them from each picture. So how do you control what your model pays attention to?

You'll find out by running one experiment three times. Same classes, same settings, same Train Model button. Only the examples change, and you'll watch the model's behavior change with them.

#What you need

  • Three paper items: say an envelope, a sheet of newspaper, and a cardboard tube.
  • Three plastic items: say a water bottle, a yogurt cup, and a plastic bag.
  • One more of each, kept hidden: a paper cup or cereal box, and a different plastic container. These are your secret test objects. They never go in front of the camera during training.
  • An empty patch of desk.

No objects handy? Do the same experiment with drawings: pencil sketches versus pen sketches work, or apples versus oranges from photos you take.

#Step 1: Plan the dataset on paper

Write this in your journal before touching the computer:

Class Objects used for training Secret test object
Paper envelope, newspaper, tube cereal box
Plastic bottle, yogurt cup, bag different container
Empty the empty desk the desk with a pencil on it

Then write a labeling rule for the hard cases. Is a paper cup with a plastic lining paper? Is a bottle with a paper label plastic? Decide now ("anything with a plastic body is Plastic") so you label the same way every time.

The secret test objects are the most important part of this plan. A model's score on things it trained on tells you almost nothing. Its score on things it has never seen is the score that counts.

#Step 2: Round 1, a narrow dataset

  1. Start a new Image Project (Standard image model).
  2. Rename the classes Paper, Plastic, and Empty (use Add a class for the third).
  3. For Paper, record only the envelope: hold it still, close to the camera, same angle, about 50 samples.
  4. For Plastic, record only the water bottle, the same way.
  5. For Empty, record the empty desk, about 50 samples.
  6. Click Train Model.

Point the camera at the envelope and the bottle. It works, of course. Now save this version (Download project as file, m3-sorter-v1.tm) before you test.

#Step 3: Test Round 1 with the secret objects

Predict first: will the cereal box be called Paper? Write it down. Then show each secret object, in two positions each, and record the top class:

Test Prediction Round 1 result Round 2 result
Cereal box, close Paper
Cereal box, far Paper
Other plastic container, close Plastic
Other plastic container, far Plastic
Desk with a pencil Empty

Expect several misses. The model learned from exactly one paper object and one plastic object. As far as it knows, "Paper" means that envelope at that distance. A cereal box shares the material but almost nothing in the picture.

#Step 4: Round 2, varied examples

Keep the same project. For each class, add samples, and keep the old ones:

  • Paper: record the newspaper and the tube too. Rotate each object while recording. Move it closer and farther. Tilt the camera a little.
  • Plastic: add the yogurt cup and the bag the same way.
  • Empty: record the desk with the lamp on and off, and from a slightly different angle.
  • Keep the class sizes roughly equal (around 150 each).

Don't touch Advanced. Click Train Model, then run exactly the same five tests and fill in the Round 2 column.

The scores should rise. Nothing about the model changed: the same pre-trained network computed features in the same way, and the training settings were identical. The only difference is that the one thing all the Paper examples now share is being paper-like, rather than being a particular envelope. Save as m3-sorter-v2.tm.

#Step 5: Round 3, plant a shortcut and catch it

Now break the model on purpose, to see what it really learns.

  1. Open the menu and choose New Project, then make an image project with classes Paper and Plastic only.
  2. Record every Paper sample with the object held in your hand.
  3. Record every Plastic sample with the object sitting on the desk, no hand in view.
  4. Train.

Before you test, predict: if you hold a plastic bottle in your hand, what will the model say?

Try it. Most likely: Paper. Then put a paper item on the desk without your hand: probably Plastic.

The model did exactly what it was asked: find whatever reliably separates the two piles. In these examples, "a hand is in the picture" separated them perfectly, and it's much easier to spot than paper versus plastic. Your class names said one thing; your examples taught another. When a model latches onto a feature that happens to go with the label in the training data but isn't the real reason, that's called a shortcut, and it's one of the most common ways real models fail.

#Step 6: See it as a table

Put the three rounds side by side:

Round What the examples had in common What the model learned
1 one object, one distance per class "that envelope" versus "that bottle"
2 many objects, angles, and lighting closer to paper-ness versus plastic-ness
3 hand in every Paper picture, never in Plastic hand versus no hand

That's the lesson of Module 3 in one table: a model learns whatever is consistent within each class and different between classes. Your job, when you can't choose features, is to make sure the only consistent difference is the one you mean.

#The finished project

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why did you keep the cereal box and the extra container hidden during training?

  • Two extra objects make almost no difference to training time.

  • A model can do well on its own training objects without having learned the idea. Only unseen objects reveal that.

  • There's no such limit; you can record as many as you like.

Show answer

B. A model can do well on its own training objects without having learned the idea. Only unseen objects reveal that.

2In Round 2 you changed only the examples, and the scores went up. What does that show?

  • The network and the training settings were identical. The new variety gave the model a better pattern to find.

  • Not always. Round 3 could have had thousands of samples and still learned "hand versus no hand".

  • It was trained correctly on narrow examples. It learned exactly what those examples showed.

Show answer

A. The network and the training settings were identical. The new variety gave the model a better pattern to find.

3A friend's sorter calls everything on their kitchen counter "Plastic". All their Plastic samples were recorded on the counter and all their Paper samples on the table. What's the best fix?

  • The model never reads the names.

  • More training on the same examples makes the shortcut stronger, not weaker.

  • When the background appears in both classes, it no longer separates them, so the model has to rely on the objects.

Show answer

C. When the background appears in both classes, it no longer separates them, so the model has to rely on the objects.

Key takeaways

  • In Teachable Machine you choose examples, not features, so the examples are how you steer the model.
  • Test on secret objects the model never trained on; that's the only score that counts.
  • Variety in angle, distance, lighting, and object makes the real idea the only thing each class has in common.
  • A model learns any consistent difference between classes, including shortcuts like hands or backgrounds.
  • Change one thing per round and keep the settings fixed, so you know what caused the change.

#Extend it

  • Add a Metal class with cans and foil. Which plastic items get confused with it?
  • Test your Round 2 model in another room. If it drops, add samples from that room and retest.
  • Ask a friend to bring three objects you've never seen. They're the toughest secret test set you can get.

#Further reading

  • Data Collection and Evaluation (Google People + AI Guidebook) (opens in a new tab): how professional teams plan what examples to collect, written for designers rather than programmers.
  • Teachable Machine FAQ: "Why isn't it working like I want it to?" (opens in a new tab): Google's suggestions for confusing a model on purpose, including changing backgrounds and showing a drawing of the object.
