m3-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn a real situation into a table of examples, features, and a label.
  • Choose the right label column for a question, and drop columns that leak it.
  • Check whether each feature exists at the moment a prediction is needed.
  • Predict which shortcut a model will learn from a described dataset.
  • Read a decision boundary and say which predictions deserve the least trust.

Every exercise here is a thinking exercise. Write your answer in your journal, then open the solution. If your answer differs, the solution's reasoning matters more than its exact wording.

#Warm-up

A pizza shop wants to predict how many minutes late each delivery will be. It has a table with one row per past delivery and these columns: distance (km), time of day, raining (yes/no), driver's name, minutes late.

What is one example? Which columns are features? Which is the label? What kind of task is it?

Show solution

One example is one past delivery (one row). The features are distance, time of day, raining, and driver's name. The label is minutes late. Because the label is a number on a scale, it's regression.

#Exercise 1: From a description to a table

A school's bird feeder has a camera. Each time something lands, the camera saves a photo, the time, and the temperature. A volunteer later writes the species under each photo. The club wants a model that names the species automatically.

Sketch the table with three made-up rows. Mark the features and the label.

Need a hint?

The volunteer's writing is the part the model must learn to produce.

Show solution
Photo Time Temperature (°C) Species (label)
photo_001.jpg 07:42 4 Blue jay
photo_002.jpg 07:45 4 Chickadee
photo_003.jpg 12:10 9 Squirrel

The photo, time, and temperature are features. The species is the label, supplied by the volunteer. Notice that "Squirrel" is a label too: if squirrels visit, the model needs that class, or it will force every squirrel into some bird species, just like the empty room in Module 1.

#Exercise 2: One table, three questions

A class keeps a table with these columns for each student:

hours of sleep · minutes of homework per night · plays a sport · attended the review session · test score

For each question, name the label column and say whether any other column should be removed:

  1. Predict a student's test score.
  2. Predict whether a student will attend the review session, a week before it happens.
  3. Group students by habits to plan study groups, with no particular answer in mind.
Need a hint?

For question 2, think about which columns exist a week before the session. For question 3, check whether there's a label at all.

Show solution
  1. Label: test score (regression). Keep the rest as features.
  2. Label: attended the review session (classification). Remove test score: the test comes after the session, so a week before, nobody knows it.
  3. No label: this is clustering. All the habit columns are used to find groups. You might drop test score, so the groups are about habits rather than results, but that's a choice about what you want the groups to mean.

#Exercise 3: Spot the feature from the future

On Monday morning, a school wants to predict which students will miss the Friday field-trip bus. A team proposes these features. Mark each one as usable or not, with a reason.

  1. Number of times the student was late this term.
  2. Friday's weather forecast, as known on Monday.
  3. Whether the student was absent on Thursday.
  4. Whether the student's permission slip has been returned.
  5. Whether the student was marked "missed bus" on Friday.
Need a hint?

Picture yourself on Monday morning. Which of these could you look up right now?

Show solution
  1. Usable. It's known on Monday and plausibly related.
  2. Usable. The forecast exists on Monday, even if it's later wrong. (Friday's actual weather would not be usable.)
  3. Not usable. Thursday hasn't happened yet on Monday.
  4. Usable, if you record its status as of Monday. Probably the strongest feature.
  5. Not usable, and dangerous. That's the label itself. A model with this column would score perfectly in training and be useless in real life. This is leakage in its purest form.

#Exercise 4: Predict what the model learns

A researcher collects 20 photos of huskies and 20 of wolves. Every wolf photo happens to have snow in the background. Almost none of the husky photos do. A model trained on these scores well on more photos taken the same way.

  1. What has the model most likely learned?
  2. What would it say about a husky photographed in snow?
  3. How would you fix the dataset?
Need a hint?

Look for something that's in every photo of one class and missing from the other, that isn't the animal.

Show solution
  1. Most likely snow versus no snow. Snow is a large, easy-to-spot difference that separates the classes perfectly in this data.
  2. Wolf. The shortcut says "snow means wolf".
  3. Collect wolves without snow and huskies with snow, so the background appears in both classes and stops separating them. Then test on new photos chosen to break the shortcut.

This isn't hypothetical. In a well-known 2016 study ("Why Should I Trust You?"), researchers deliberately trained a husky-versus-wolf classifier on photos like these, and their explanation tool showed it was mostly using the snow. It's the same trap as the hand in your Round 3 sorter.

#Exercise 5: Write a labeling rule

Three volunteers labeled the same 100 banana photos as Ripe or Not ripe. They disagreed on 23 photos: mostly bananas with a few brown spots, and bananas that were yellow with green tips.

Write a labeling rule all three could follow, and say what to do with photos that still don't fit.

Need a hint?

A good rule names something visible in the photo and settles the two problem cases explicitly.

Show solution

One workable rule:

  • Ripe: the peel is mostly yellow (no green visible except possibly at the very stem) and has at most scattered brown spots.
  • Not ripe: any green on the body or tips.
  • Exclude (don't label): photos where the banana is mostly brown, blurry, or covered by something.

What matters is less the exact rule than having one, writing it down, and re-checking that labelers now agree. If the volunteers still disagree on a case, the model will learn a blur of their opinions on exactly those photos. Teachable Machine's home page has a "Bananameter" tutorial built around this very problem.

#Exercise 6: Read a decision boundary

A mango sorter learned from 40 mangoes, each measured for firmness and skin color. The chart shows its decision boundary and four new mangoes, A to D.

  1. What does the model predict for each of A, B, C, and D?
  2. Which two predictions would you trust least, and why?
Need a hint?

Trust drops in two different places: near the line, and far from every training mango. Find one of each.

Show solution
  1. A: Ripe (orange region). B: Unripe (blue region). C: Ripe, barely: it sits almost on the line. D: Ripe, just inside the orange region.
  2. C and D, for different reasons.
    • C is on the boundary. A tiny measuring error, like pressing slightly harder when testing firmness, would flip the answer. The model is close to a coin toss here.
    • D is far from every training mango. No training mango was both rock hard and fully orange. Maybe it's a different variety, or a plastic decoration. The model still answers, because the boundary extends forever, but it has no experience to back the answer up. A model's predictions are most reliable where its training examples were.

Module 5 turns these two kinds of doubt into a careful look at confidence scores.

#Challenge: Plan a door-watching dataset

Your class wants a Teachable Machine model that looks at a webcam photo of the classroom door and says Open or Closed. Plan the dataset on one page:

  • The classes (are two enough?) and a labeling rule for "half open".
  • How many samples per class, and what you'll vary while recording.
  • A secret test set: what it contains and when you'll record it.
  • One shortcut the model could learn by accident, and how your plan prevents it.
Need a hint?

Think about what else changes in the photos between times the door is open and closed. Who tends to be in the doorway? What does the light from the hallway do?

Show solution

An example plan:

  • Classes: Open, Closed, and Blocked (someone standing in the doorway), so a person isn't forced into Open or Closed. Rule: "Open means you can see the hallway floor through the gap; otherwise Closed."
  • Samples: about 100 per class, recorded at different times of day, with hallway lights on and off, with the door open at several angles, and with people walking past in both classes.
  • Secret test set: 20 photos per class taken on a different day, never added to training.
  • Shortcut to prevent: hallway light. If the door is only ever open when the hallway lights are on, the model may learn "bright = open". Recording open-door samples with the hallway dark (and closed-door samples while light leaks under the door) breaks the link. A second shortcut: the clock on the wall shows different times in each class if you record all the Open samples first. Mixing the recording times fixes that.

m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why a model must be scored on examples it never trained on.
  • Describe what training, validation, and test sets are each for.
  • Recognize overfitting on a chart of training and test error.
  • Spot test sets that aren't really new, like near-duplicate photos.
  • Describe a neuron as a weighted vote, and learning as nudging weights to reduce error.

Two students prepare for a history test. One studies the topics. The other finds last year's answer key and memorizes it: question 1 is B, question 2 is D. On last year's test, the memorizer scores 100%. On this year's test, with the questions reworded, they score 40%. The first student scores 85% on both.

If you only ever graded them on last year's test, you'd pick the wrong student. Models can memorize too, and they can fool you in exactly the same way. This lesson is about how to grade a model fairly, and then about what's actually happening inside one when it "learns".

#Hold some examples back

The fix is simple to say: before training, set some labeled examples aside and never let the model see them. After training, score the model on those. They play the role of this year's test.

In practice, data is usually split three ways:

  • Training set: what the model learns from.
  • Validation set: what you use to make choices, like how long to train or which version of the model to keep. Every time you peek at a score and change something, you're learning from that set too.
  • Test set: locked away until the very end. One score, reported honestly. If you keep tweaking until the test score looks good, it has quietly become a validation set, and you no longer have an honest score.

Teachable Machine does a simpler version automatically. Its "Under the hood" panel explains that it splits your samples into two buckets: 85% for training and 15% as test samples that "are never used to train the model". You'll look at those charts in the next lesson.

#Overfitting: memorizing the noise

Here's a pattern hidden in some noisy measurements (it happens to be a smooth wave). Each panel fits a model with a different amount of freedom to bend, using only the filled-in training points, then checks it against the hollow test points it never saw:

Left: a straight line can't bend, so it misses the wave on both training and test points. That's underfitting: the model is too simple for the pattern.

Middle: a gently curving model follows the wave and lands close to the test points it never saw. Low error on both.

Right: a model allowed to bend nine times threads through every training point exactly, so its training error is 0.00. But to do it, it learned the random noise in those ten points, and it swings wildly between them. Its test error is the worst of the three. That's overfitting: excellent on the examples it trained on, poor on new ones. It's the memorizer with the answer key.

Now repeat that experiment on 200 fresh datasets for every amount of bendiness from 0 (a flat line) to 7, and plot the typical errors:

This is the most important chart in machine learning, and it's worth reading slowly. The blue line only ever goes down: more freedom always fits the training examples better. If that were the only number you looked at, you'd always pick the most complicated model. The orange line falls at first, as the model gains enough freedom to capture the wave, then turns back up once the extra freedom is spent on memorizing noise. The best model is at the bottom of the orange curve, and you can only find it with examples the model didn't train on.

#When the test set isn't really new

Holding examples back only works if they're truly different from the training ones. Some ways a test set secretly isn't:

  • Near-duplicates. Teachable Machine's webcam records many frames per second. Two frames a fraction of a second apart are practically the same picture. If one lands in training and its twin in the test bucket, the "test" is a memory check.
  • The same person, place, or object on both sides. A gesture model tested on photos of the same hands, in the same room, says little about other hands in other rooms.
  • Information from the future. A model that predicts tomorrow's attendance shouldn't be tested on days that came before its training days.

When test examples leak information from training, the score comes out too good. You'll see this happen inside Teachable Machine in the next lesson, and Module 5 builds a stress test that gets around it.

#A neuron is a weighted vote

Teachable Machine's model is a neural network. Under the name, the basic part is simple. A single neuron takes some input numbers, multiplies each by a weight that says how much it matters, adds them up with an extra number called a bias, and squashes the total into a range like 0 to 1.

Think of deciding whether to go to the park. Inputs: how sunny it is, whether friends are going, whether homework is done. Weights: friends might matter a lot (a big weight), sunshine a little. The bias is your general mood: a bit lazy today means the total has to be higher before you go.

Here's one neuron with a single input, drawn three ways:

Compare blue and orange: same flip point (input 5), but the bigger weight makes orange snap from "no" to "yes" almost instantly. Compare blue and green: same weight, but the bias moves the flip point from 5 down to 2. A neuron is a dimmer switch whose sharpness and position are set by its weight and bias.

A network stacks thousands or millions of these in layers. The outputs of one layer are the inputs to the next, so later neurons can respond to combinations: not just "edge here", but "edges arranged like a thumb". The final layer has one output per class; those are your Output bars.

#Learning means nudging the weights

Nobody sets those millions of weights by hand. They start out random, and training adjusts them. The recipe:

  1. Show the network an example and let it guess.
  2. Measure how wrong the guess was. That number is the error (Teachable Machine's charts call it loss).
  3. Nudge every weight a tiny bit in whichever direction would have made the error smaller.
  4. Repeat, many thousands of times.

Here's the smallest possible version: a model with one weight, learning how many minutes a delivery takes per kilometer. The examples were all made at exactly 5 minutes per km, but the model starts out guessing 0. Step through it and watch w and error:

Early on, guesses are far too low, so error is a big negative number, and the nudge pushes w up a lot. As w approaches 5, the errors shrink, and so do the nudges. After four passes it's close to 5, and nobody told it the answer. The same three ideas appear in Teachable Machine's Advanced panel:

  • Epochs (50 by default): how many full passes through the training examples. Our loop had 4.
  • Learning Rate (0.001 by default): the size of each nudge, our rate. Too small and learning crawls; too big and the weights overshoot back and forth. Teachable Machine's own tooltip warns that even small changes can have huge effects.
  • Batch Size (16 by default): how many examples are looked at together before each nudge. Our loop nudged after every single example.

In a real network the hard part is step 3: working out the right direction for millions of weights at once. The method that does it is called backpropagation, and the second video below shows the "walking downhill" idea behind it.

⚠️ Watch out

Scoring a model on its own training examples. It's the most common mistake in machine learning, and it always looks like success: the right-hand panel above scored a perfect 0.00. A score only means something on examples the model didn't train on.

⚠️ Watch out

"More training is always better." More epochs drive training error down, but past a point the model starts fitting noise and test error goes up. Watch the test line, not the training line.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A model scores 99% on its training examples and 61% on the test set. What's the best description?

  • An underfit model does poorly on training examples too. This one aces them.

  • A big gap between training and test performance is the signature of overfitting.

  • A low test score is the test set doing its job: revealing what the training score hid.

Show answer

B. A big gap between training and test performance is the signature of overfitting.

2You try 12 different settings, check the test score after each, and keep the best one. Why is that final test score too optimistic?

  • Trying many settings is fine. The problem is which set of examples you chose them with.

  • You picked the setting that happened to suit those particular test examples. An honest final score needs examples that played no part in any choice.

  • They don't drift by themselves; the issue is how the score was used.

Show answer

B. You picked the setting that happened to suit those particular test examples. An honest final score needs examples that played no part in any choice.

3Using the neuron chart: which change makes a neuron flip from "no" to "yes" at a lower input, without changing how sharp the flip is?

  • A bigger weight makes the switch sharper, like the orange curve.

  • The green curve kept weight 1 but changed the bias, which slid the flip point from 5 to 2.

  • The learning rate controls how training nudges the weights, not the shape of a finished neuron.

Show answer

B. The green curve kept weight 1 but changed the bias, which slid the flip point from 5 to 2.

4In the trace, what would happen if rate were much bigger, say 0.2?

  • With a big learning rate, a large error causes a huge nudge that jumps past the answer. Teachable Machine's tooltip warns about exactly this.

  • The nudge depends on the error and the distance, so a bigger rate overshoots rather than landing exactly.

  • The examples are the same, but the size of each step changes, and so does where the steps land.

Show answer

A. With a big learning rate, a large error causes a huge nudge that jumps past the answer. Teachable Machine's tooltip warns about exactly this.

Key takeaways

  • Score a model only on examples it never trained on; the training score always flatters it.
  • Training set to learn, validation set to choose settings, test set for one honest final score.
  • Overfitting shows up as training error falling while test error rises.
  • Near-duplicate examples split across training and test make a score look better than it is.
  • A neuron is a weighted vote squashed into 0 to 1; training nudges weights to reduce error. Epochs, learning rate, and batch size control that process.

#Further reading

  • Dividing the original dataset (Google ML Crash Course) (opens in a new tab): a clear page on training, validation, and test sets, with good advice about duplicates.
  • TensorFlow Playground (opens in a new tab): a real neural network training in your browser. Press play, watch the weights (the lines) change, and try making the network bigger or the learning rate larger.
  • Neural networks (3Blue1Brown) (opens in a new tab): the written lessons that go with the videos, if you prefer reading.

m4-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Train a neural network in TensorFlow Playground and read its training loss and test loss.
  • Explain what the neurons, lines, and background colors show while it learns.
  • Make a network overfit on purpose by changing the data split, the noise, and the network size.
  • Fix overfitting three ways, changing one thing at a time and recording the result.
  • Connect the Playground's two loss numbers to the charts in Teachable Machine's Under the hood panel.

Teachable Machine hides its network. You press Train Model and a minute later it works, but you never see a neuron. Today you'll use a different free tool, TensorFlow Playground, made by Google researchers to show exactly what a small network is doing while it learns. Every neuron is a little picture, every weight is a line, and two numbers at the top right tell you how it's doing on training data and on test data.

You'll train one network that works, then deliberately build one that memorizes, then fix it. By the end you'll have a page of journal notes like this:

Run What I changed Training loss Test loss Verdict
1 Defaults, Circle data
2 Noisy data, 10% training, big network
3 Training data back up to 70%

#Step 1: Open the Playground and find the controls

Go to playground.tensorflow.org. It runs in any modern browser, needs no account, and, as the page itself promises, you can't break it. You'll see:

  • Top bar: a play button (Run/Pause), a reset button, a step button, the Epoch counter, and drop-downs for Learning rate (0.03), Activation (Tanh), Regularization, and Problem type (Classification).
  • Data (left): four small pictures under "Which dataset do you want to use?" (Circle, Exclusive or, Gaussian, Spiral), then sliders for Ratio of training to test data (50%), Noise (0), and Batch size (10).
  • Features: inputs the network gets. By default only X1 and X2, a dot's horizontal and vertical position, are on.
  • Hidden layers (middle): two layers, of 4 and 2 neurons, with + and − buttons to add or remove layers and neurons.
  • Output (right): Test loss and Training loss, a small chart of both over time, and a big picture of the data.

The colors follow one rule: blue means positive, orange means negative. Each dot is an example, labeled blue or orange. The background shows what the network predicts for every spot, and stronger color means a more confident prediction.

#Step 2: Train the default network

Leave everything as it is (Circle dataset: a blue cluster surrounded by an orange ring). Press play.

Watch three things for about 20 seconds:

  1. The background. It starts as a blur and quickly forms a blue blob in the middle with orange around it. That's the decision boundary from Module 3, forming live.
  2. The lines between neurons. They change thickness and color as training nudges the weights. Thick means a large weight; blue lines are positive weights and orange lines negative.
  3. The two losses. Both fall toward zero and stay close together.

Press pause after a few hundred epochs. Write the epoch count, training loss, and test loss in Run 1 of your journal.

Remember the trace in the last lesson, where one weight crept toward 5? This network has a couple of dozen weights, and every one of them was being nudged at the same time, epoch after epoch, in whatever direction lowered the loss.

#Step 3: Look inside the neurons

Hover over a neuron in the first hidden layer. A larger version of its picture appears on the right. Each first-layer neuron draws a straight split across the data: blue on one side, orange on the other. It's one weighted vote of X1 and X2, exactly like the neuron chart from the last lesson, just with two inputs instead of one.

Now hover over a neuron in the second layer. Its picture has curved edges. It combined several straight splits from the first layer into something more complex. That's the whole idea of depth: each layer builds on the pieces made by the layer before it, which is how a deep network goes from edges to shapes to "thumbs up".

🧪 Try it yourself

Remove neurons with the − button until the first layer has only 1, then press reset and play. A single straight split can't surround a circle, so the losses stay high. Add neurons back until it works. How many does the circle need?

#Step 4: Make it overfit on purpose

Now set up the conditions for memorizing. Press reset, then change these one by one:

  1. Click the Gaussian dataset (two clusters, blue and orange).
  2. Drag Noise up to 50. The clusters now overlap, with many dots on the "wrong" side. Those are the noisy examples.
  3. Drag Ratio of training to test data down to 10%, so the network learns from very few dots.
  4. Make the network big: add hidden layers until there are 4, and give each layer 8 neurons.
  5. Tick Show test data under the output, so you can see the dots the network never trains on.

Before pressing play, predict in your journal: will the training loss and test loss stay together, as in Run 1?

Now press play and let it run for at least 1,000 epochs. In most runs, you'll see the training loss keep dropping while the test loss stops improving and then creeps up. Look at the background: little islands and fingers of color appear around individual training dots. The network is bending its boundary to swallow single noisy examples. It's the "memorized" panel from the last lesson, with a real network.

Record Run 2. Your exact numbers will differ (every run starts from different random weights), but the gap between the two losses is what matters.

⚠️ Watch out

"The training loss is tiny, so it's a great model." That's the trap. The training loss only tells you how well it fits the dots it learned from. With noisy data and few examples, a low training loss and a rising test loss means memorizing. Always read both numbers.

#Step 5: Fix it three ways, one change at a time

Starting from the Run 2 settings each time, change exactly one thing, press reset and play, and record training loss and test loss after about the same number of epochs as Run 2:

  1. More data. Drag Ratio of training to test data back up to 70%. With more examples, single noisy dots matter less, and the boundary smooths out.
  2. A smaller network. Back to 10% data, but cut the network to 1 hidden layer with 2 neurons. It doesn't have enough freedom to wrap around individual dots.
  3. Stop early. Back to the big network and 10% data. Watch the test loss and press pause when it's at its lowest, before it starts climbing. You keep the version that was best on new data.

Which fix gave the lowest test loss in your runs? There's no single right answer. All three show the same principle from the curve in the last lesson: you want the model that does best on data it hasn't seen, not the one that fits its training data most perfectly.

💡 Tip

Changing one thing per run is what makes your journal useful. If you changed the data and the network size at once and the test loss improved, you'd have no idea which change did it.

#Step 6: Push the learning rate

Go back to the defaults by typing playground.tensorflow.org into the address bar again. (Reloading isn't enough: the Playground saves your settings in the page's address, after the #.) Set Learning rate to 3 and press play. The background flickers and the loss jumps around instead of settling: each nudge is so large it overshoots. Then try 0.0001: almost nothing happens for a long time, because each nudge is tiny. The default, 0.03, sits in between. This is the same overshooting you'll see in the practice lesson, live.

#Step 7: Find the same two lines in Teachable Machine

Open your recycling sorter from Module 3 (Open project from file). Under Train Model, open Advanced, click Under the hood, and train again. Teachable Machine draws Accuracy per epoch and Loss per epoch, each with a training line and a test line, just like the Playground's two numbers. Its test samples are a random 15% of your samples.

Notice one difference. In the Playground, test dots are drawn from the same pattern but are truly separate examples. In Teachable Machine, your samples are webcam frames recorded a split second apart, so the 15% test bucket is full of near-twins of training frames. That's why its test line can look excellent even for a model that fails in another room. Module 5 builds a proper stress test for that.

#The finished journal page

Check your understanding

3 questions

1In Run 2, training loss is 0.05 and test loss is 0.45 and rising. What's happening?

  • An underfit network does badly on training data too. This one fits its training dots very well.

  • A large and growing gap between training loss and test loss is the signature of overfitting.

  • The test dots come from the same pattern. They're revealing what the training loss hides.

Show answer

B. A large and growing gap between training loss and test loss is the signature of overfitting.

2Why did you change only one setting per run in Step 5?

  • If two things change at once, you can't tell which one helped or hurt.

  • You can change as many settings as you like; the limit is your ability to explain the result.

  • Changing fewer settings doesn't affect speed.

Show answer

A. If two things change at once, you can't tell which one helped or hurt.

3A first-layer neuron's picture shows a straight split, but a second-layer neuron's picture has curves. Why?

  • They do the same weighted sum and squash. The difference is what they receive.

  • Mixing several straight splits, each with its own weight, can produce curved and closed shapes.

  • Every layer trains for the same number of epochs.

Show answer

B. Mixing several straight splits, each with its own weight, can produce curved and closed shapes.

Key takeaways

  • TensorFlow Playground shows a real network learning: neurons as pictures, weights as lines, and the boundary as background color.
  • Early layers draw simple splits; later layers combine them into complex shapes.
  • Overfitting shows up as training loss falling while test loss rises, and it's most likely with noisy data, few examples, and a big network.
  • More data, a smaller network, and stopping early all reduce overfitting; test one change at a time.
  • Teachable Machine's Under the hood charts show the same training and test lines, but near-duplicate webcam frames can make its test line too optimistic.

#Extend it

  • Try the Spiral dataset with only X1 and X2 as features. Then switch on more features (like sin(X1) and sin(X2)) and see how much smaller a network can solve it.
  • Change Regularization to L2 with a Regularization rate of 0.03 on your Run 2 settings. It's a fourth fix: it penalizes large weights, so the boundary stays smoother.

  • Neural networks: interactive exercises (Google ML Crash Course) (opens in a new tab): guided Playground challenges with answers, a good next step after this lesson.
  • Interpreting loss curves (Google ML Crash Course) (opens in a new tab): a gallery of real loss charts and what each shape usually means.

m4-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Find the leak in an evaluation that makes a score look better than it is.
  • Diagnose underfitting and overfitting from training and test curves.
  • Split a dataset so the test set is truly new, including splitting by person.
  • Compute a neuron's weighted vote by hand and decide which weight a mistake should nudge.
  • Predict the effect of the learning rate and the number of epochs.

These exercises mix the two halves of Module 4: testing fairly, and how networks learn. As always, write your answer before you open a solution.

#Warm-up

Match each set to its job: training set, validation set, test set.

  1. Used once, at the very end, for the score you report.
  2. What the model's weights learn from.
  3. What you check while choosing between 20 epochs and 50.
Show solution
  1. Test set.
  2. Training set.
  3. Validation set. If you used the test set for this, it would stop being a fair final exam.

#Exercise 1: Spot the leak

Each team reports a great test score. For each, find the reason the score is too good.

  1. A face-unlock model is trained on 20 photos of each of 50 students. The 1,000 photos are shuffled and split 80/20 into training and test.
  2. A dataset of 5,000 dog photos was collected from the web. Nobody removed duplicates, and many popular photos appear several times.
  3. A model predicts tomorrow's cafeteria attendance. One feature is "number of lunches sold", taken from the same day being predicted.
  4. A student tunes a model by checking its test score after each of 30 changes and keeps the best version.
  5. A chest X-ray model is trained and tested on scans from two hospitals. Very sick patients were mostly scanned at Hospital B, which stamps its name in the corner of every scan.
Need a hint?

For each, ask: what does the test set share with the training set, or what does the model know that it couldn't know in real use?

Show solution
  1. The same faces are in both sets. Each student has about 16 photos in training and 4 in test, so the test asks "do you recognize photos of people you've already seen?" For a model that must work on new people, split by student.
  2. Duplicates cross the split. A photo in the test set may have an identical copy in training. Remove duplicates before splitting.
  3. A feature from the future. Lunches sold on the day is only known after the day, and it's practically the answer. It wouldn't exist when the prediction is needed.
  4. The test set became a validation set. Picking the best of 30 versions by test score selects the version that happened to suit those particular test examples. A fresh test set is needed for an honest number.
  5. A shortcut. The model can learn "Hospital B's stamp means sick" instead of reading the lungs. It would score well on scans from these two hospitals and fail at a hospital with a different stamp. Researchers have found real X-ray models picking up which hospital a scan came from, so this is a real risk, not a made-up one.

#Exercise 2: Read the curves

Three models were trained for 50 epochs. Blue is accuracy on the training samples, orange on the test samples.

  1. Label each model: underfit, overfit, or healthy.
  2. For the overfit model, roughly when should training have stopped?
  3. Suggest one change for the underfit model.
Need a hint?

Look at two things: how high the training line gets, and the size of the gap between the lines.

Show solution
  1. Model A is underfit: even on its own training samples it only reaches about 58%. It can't capture the pattern. Model B is healthy: both lines are high and close. Model C is overfit: training accuracy hits 100% while test accuracy peaks and then slides down.
  2. Around epoch 12, where the orange line peaks. Every epoch after that makes the model better at its training samples and worse at new ones. Stopping at the best validation score is a standard technique called early stopping.
  3. For A: give the model more to work with. Better features or examples (classes that actually look different), a more flexible model, or more training if the lines are still rising. Training longer alone won't help much here, since both lines have flattened.

#Exercise 3: Split by person

A club is building a Teachable Machine model that recognizes five sign-language letters. Thirty students each recorded 20 photos of each letter: 3,000 photos. The model must work for students who join next year.

Describe how to split the photos into training, validation, and test sets.

Need a hint?

Who is the model for? The test set should contain the kind of examples the model will meet in real use.

Show solution

Split by student, not by photo. For example: photos from 20 students for training, 5 students for validation, and 5 students for the test set. Each student's photos go entirely into one set.

If you split photos randomly, every student's hands appear in all three sets, and the test score measures "recognizing hands it has already seen". Next year's students are new people, so the test set must be made of people the model has never seen. It's also worth checking that the 5 test students differ in ways that matter: hand size, skin tone, left- and right-handedness, and the rooms they recorded in.

#Exercise 4: A neuron, by hand

A neuron decides whether to bring an umbrella. It has three inputs, three weights, and a bias:

Input Weight
Cloudy now (0 or 1) 1.0
Forecast chance of rain (0 to 1) 4.0
Walking more than 10 minutes (0 or 1) 1.5
Bias −3.0

Total = (each input × its weight, added up) + bias. If the total is above 0, bring the umbrella.

  1. Morning 1: cloudy, 30% rain forecast, long walk. Umbrella or not?
  2. Morning 2: clear sky, 60% rain forecast, short walk. Umbrella or not?
  3. On Morning 2 it poured and you got soaked. During training, which weight should get the biggest nudge, and in which direction?
Need a hint?

For Morning 2, two of the three inputs are 0. A weight multiplied by an input of 0 had no effect on the decision.

Show solution
  1. Umbrella. 1×1.0 + 0.3×4.0 + 1×1.5 − 3.0 = 0.7, which is above 0.
  2. No umbrella. 0 + 0.6×4.0 + 0 − 3.0 = −0.6, below 0.
  3. Increase the rain-chance weight (and possibly make the bias less negative). Only the rain-chance input was non-zero, so it's the only weight that contributed to the wrong answer. Cloudy and long walk were 0, so changing their weights wouldn't have changed Morning 2's total at all. That's why, in the nudge rule from the trace in Lesson 1 (w = w - rate * error * km), the nudge is multiplied by the input: inputs that were zero get no blame.

#Exercise 5: Three learning rates

The same one-weight delivery model from Lesson 1 was trained three times, with learning rates 0.002, 0.02, and 0.15. All three start with the same error. Which run used which rate?

Need a hint?

A tiny step size makes steady but slow progress. A huge one jumps past the answer, and each overshoot can be bigger than the last.

Show solution
  • Run Y used 0.002. The steps are tiny, so error falls steadily but slowly: still about 7 minutes off after 10 epochs.
  • Run Z used 0.02, the rate from the Lesson 1 trace. Error drops to nearly zero within four epochs.
  • Run X used 0.15. Each nudge overshoots 5 minutes per km by more than the last, so error grows instead of shrinking. That's called diverging, and it's why Teachable Machine's tooltip says to be careful with the learning rate.

There's no single "right" learning rate; it depends on the model and the data. But the shapes are worth recognizing: slow and steady means too small, exploding means too big.

#Exercise 6: Predict what Teachable Machine will do

For each experiment with your recycling sorter from Module 3, predict what the Accuracy per epoch chart will show, then explain why.

  1. Epochs set to 1.
  2. A fresh copy with only 10 samples per class, and Epochs set to 300.
  3. Learning Rate changed from 0.001 to 1.
Need a hint?

Use the three ideas from Lesson 1: underfitting, overfitting, and the size of each nudge.

Show solution
  1. A single point, probably low or middling. One pass isn't enough nudging for the final layer to settle, so the model is likely underfit. (The pre-trained features are good, so it may do better than you'd guess.)
  2. Training accuracy hits 100% early and stays there; test accuracy is jumpy. With 10 samples per class, the 15% test bucket is only one or two samples per class, so each one is worth a huge chunk of the score. With so few examples, overfitting is likely, but the test line is too noisy to show it reliably. The fix is more (and more varied) samples, not more epochs.
  3. Erratic or stuck accuracy, and loss that jumps around or grows. Steps 1,000 times larger than the default overshoot, like Run X above. Some runs may still land somewhere reasonable by luck, which is exactly why you shouldn't trust one run. Click Reset Defaults afterward.

If you have time, try all three and compare against your predictions in your journal.

#Challenge: An evaluation plan for a bus-stop camera

A school wants a model that looks at a camera photo of the bus stop and says Bus here or No bus, so students can stay inside until it arrives. Write a one-page evaluation plan:

  • Where the training examples come from, and over what period.
  • How you'll split the data so the test set is honest. Think about time, weather, and near-duplicate frames.
  • What you'll measure. Is accuracy enough, or does one kind of mistake matter more?
  • A result that would make you say "don't use this yet".
Need a hint?

Which is worse: the model saying "Bus here" when there's no bus, or "No bus" when the bus is there? Who pays for each mistake?

Show solution

An example plan:

  • Training data: photos every 30 seconds for four weeks, labeled by checking the bus schedule and the photos themselves. Include rain, snow, morning darkness, and other vehicles (delivery trucks, cars) in the No bus class.
  • Split by time, not by photo: weeks 1 and 2 for training, week 3 for validation, week 4 as the test set. Splitting randomly would put frames 30 seconds apart on both sides of the split. Splitting by week also tests whether the model handles weather it didn't train on. If week 4 has no snow, say so in the report rather than claiming it works in snow.
  • Measure each mistake separately: "No bus" when the bus is there is the costly mistake, because students miss the bus. Report how often that happens, separately from overall accuracy. A model that's 97% accurate but misses one bus a week isn't good enough.
  • Don't-use-yet rule: if the test week shows even one missed bus at a time students were waiting, or if the model confuses delivery trucks with buses more than occasionally, keep a person checking, or add the bus company's GPS feed (a non-AI option that might work better on its own).

m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why a model can say 99% and still be wrong.
  • Use a threshold to turn a score into a decision, and predict what moving it does.
  • Name the four outcomes of a yes/no decision: true and false positives, true and false negatives.
  • Decide which mistake is worse in a given setting, such as a spam filter or a medical test.
  • Read accuracy for each group of people, and explain what the Gender Shades study found.

Hold a banana up to a model trained only on Thumbs up, Thumbs down, and Nothing. There's a fair chance the Preview panel shows something like Thumbs up 96%. The model has never seen a banana. It isn't 96% sure the banana is a thumb in any sense a person would mean. So what is that number?

This lesson answers that question, then follows it to a harder one. When a model is wrong, who is it wrong about? In 2018, two researchers showed that face-analysis products from three large companies were almost perfect for one group of people and wrong about a third of the time for another. Each product's headline accuracy looked fine.

#A confidence score is a split, not a promise

The bars under Output in Teachable Machine always add up to 100%. That's by design: the last step of the model takes its raw scores and squeezes them into shares of 100, one share per class. The model must hand out all 100 points, even when the picture matches none of its classes well.

So Thumbs up 96% means: "of the answers I'm allowed to give, this one fits best, by a lot." It does not mean "there's a 96% chance this is a thumbs-up." Those two statements sound alike and are very different.

Here's the precise version. A model is well calibrated if, out of all the times it says 80%, it's right about 80% of the time. Many models aren't. They tend to be overconfident, especially on inputs unlike their training examples: a banana, a new background, a face from a group that was rare in the training data. Confidence is most trustworthy on inputs that look like what the model trained on, which is exactly when you need it least.

🧪 Try it yourself

Open any Teachable Machine model you've trained. Point the camera at three objects that belong to none of your classes: a mug, a book, your ceiling. Write down the top class and its percentage each time. How many times did it go above 80%?

#Thresholds turn a score into a decision

Most real systems don't show you bars. They make a decision. A spam filter gives every email a spam score from 0 to 1, and a rule decides what happens: if the score is at least 0.5, send it to the spam folder. That cutoff is the threshold.

The chart below shows the scores a filter gave 1,000 real emails and 1,000 spam emails (made-up data, shaped like a real filter's).

Look at the middle, where blue and orange overlap. Some real emails (a newsletter, a message with lots of links) score as high as some spam. Wherever you draw the line, a few emails land on the wrong side. The only question is which wrong side you'd rather have.

Now slide the threshold from 0 to 1 and count the mistakes at every position:

The blue line falls as the threshold rises: a strict filter rarely buries a real email. The orange line climbs: the same strict filter lets more spam through. At 0.3 you lose about 300 real emails to stop nearly all the spam. At 0.7 you lose almost none but let about a third of the spam in. The lines can't both reach zero, because the piles overlap. Changing the threshold never removes mistakes. It chooses which ones you get.

#Four outcomes, and why the names matter

Any yes/no decision has four possible results. Call the thing you're looking for "positive" (spam, disease, a match):

Model says yes Model says no
Really yes True positive: caught it False negative: missed it
Really no False positive: false alarm True negative: correctly left alone

This grid is called a confusion matrix. Teachable Machine can draw one for you under Advanced › Under the hood, where it's labelled with the true Class on one axis and the Prediction on the other. Next lesson you'll build one from your own tests.

Which mistake is worse depends entirely on the setting:

  • Spam filter. A false positive hides a real email, maybe a job offer. A false negative means you delete one more junk message. Most people prefer a high threshold that lets some spam through.
  • Medical screening. A false negative sends a sick person home thinking they're fine. A false positive means a worrying phone call and a second test. Screening tests use a low threshold on purpose, and they produce many false alarms as a result: in US studies, roughly half to 60% of women who get a mammogram every year for ten years get at least one false-positive callback. Doctors accept that cost because a follow-up test sorts out most false alarms, while a missed cancer can't be undone.
  • A smoke alarm is the everyday version. It shrieks at burnt toast because a missed fire is far worse than an annoying beep.

#The number that hid the problem: Gender Shades

In 2018, Joy Buolamwini (MIT Media Lab) and Timnit Gebru (Microsoft Research) tested three commercial products that guess a person's gender from a photo, made by Microsoft, IBM, and Face++. Popular face datasets at the time were 79.6% and 86.2% lighter-skinned, so they built a balanced test set: 1,270 official photos of members of parliament from Rwanda, Senegal, South Africa, Iceland, Finland, and Sweden. A dermatologist labelled each person's skin type.

Overall, the products were right on 87.9% to 93.7% of faces. Then the researchers split the results into four groups:

Read the chart left to right. Every product did worst on darker-skinned women: one in five wrong for Microsoft, about one in three for Face++ and IBM. Every product did best, or nearly best, on lighter-skinned men, where IBM's error rate was 0.3% and Microsoft's was zero. An average of 90% hid a group getting a third of its answers wrong.

The study made news, and it had an effect: a follow-up audit by Deborah Raji and Buolamwini found the companies had narrowed the gaps in later versions. The lesson for you is the method. Never accept a single accuracy number. Ask "accurate for whom?" and split the results by the groups who will use the system.

⚠️ Watch out

Three mistakes people make with scores

  1. Reading confidence as probability of being right. "It said 98%, so it's almost certainly correct." Only if the model is well calibrated and the input looks like its training data. Test it; don't assume.
  2. Reporting one accuracy number. 94% accuracy can mean 99% for most users and 60% for a group nobody checked. Always split by group.
  3. Deleting a sensitive column and calling the data fair. Removing "race" or "gender" doesn't remove the pattern if other columns (a ZIP code, a first name, a school) carry the same information. Check the results by group, not the inputs.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A model trained on Rock, Paper, and Scissors shows Paper 97% when you hold up a sheet of homework. What's the best explanation?

  • The model can't consider "homework" at all. 97% is its share of the vote, not a probability of being right.

  • With no class for "something else", every input is forced into one of the three, often with high confidence.

  • It's working as designed. A "Nothing" or "Other" class, plus testing on unfamiliar objects, is the fix.

Show answer

B. With no class for "something else", every input is forced into one of the three, often with high confidence.

2A clinic uses a screening test for a serious disease that is easy to treat if caught early. A follow-up test is cheap and accurate. Where should the screening threshold go?

  • A false alarm costs a follow-up test. A miss costs a person their early treatment, so misses are the worse mistake here.

  • That would send more sick people home. In screening, false negatives are usually the costlier error.

  • 0.5 has no special meaning. The right threshold depends on the cost of each kind of mistake.

Show answer

A. A false alarm costs a follow-up test. A miss costs a person their early treatment, so misses are the worse mistake here.

3On the spam chart, you move the threshold from 0.5 to 0.7. What happens?

  • The lines move in opposite directions. Lowering one raises the other.

  • A stricter cutoff flags fewer emails of every kind, so fewer false positives and more false negatives.

  • That happens when you lower the threshold, not raise it.

Show answer

B. A stricter cutoff flags fewer emails of every kind, so fewer false positives and more false negatives.

4A company says its face-unlock feature is "95% accurate." What's the most useful question to ask next?

  • Training length doesn't tell you who the 5% of errors fall on.

  • An improving average can still hide a group that fails badly.

  • Gender Shades showed that a strong average can hide error rates over 30% for one group.

Show answer

C. Gender Shades showed that a strong average can hide error rates over 30% for one group.

Key takeaways

  • Confidence bars add up to 100% across the classes a model knows, so an unfamiliar input still gets a confident-looking answer.
  • A threshold turns a score into a decision. Moving it trades false positives for false negatives; it never removes both.
  • Pick the threshold by asking which mistake is worse and for whom: a hidden email, a missed illness, a false alarm.
  • A single accuracy number can hide large gaps. Split results by group before trusting a system.
  • Gender Shades (2018) found error rates up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women and under 1% for lighter-skinned men in the same products.

#Further reading

  • Gender Shades paper (Buolamwini and Gebru, 2018) (opens in a new tab): the original study. Table 4 has every number in the chart above.
  • Thresholds and the confusion matrix (opens in a new tab): Google's Machine Learning Crash Course page, with an interactive threshold slider.
  • Measuring Fairness (opens in a new tab): an interactive essay from Google's PAIR team showing why you can't make every fairness measure equal at once.

m5-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Train a Rock, Paper, Scissors, and Nothing model in Teachable Machine.
  • Explain why Teachable Machine's built-in accuracy is too optimistic for real use.
  • Plan and run a stress test across lighting, background, and a second person's hand.
  • Read a confusion matrix and an accuracy-by-condition chart built from your own log.
  • Choose a confidence threshold and say who it helps and who it costs.

Your rock-paper-scissors model scores 100% on Teachable Machine's own test. Then your friend tries it and it calls their rock "Paper, 88%". Both results are true. They answer different questions: the first asks "does it work on pictures like the ones I trained on?", and the second asks "does it work for the people who will actually use it?"

You're going to answer the second question properly. By the end you'll have a one-page model report card like this:

The charts in this lesson use one tester's log. Your numbers will differ, and that's the point: run your own tests and compare.

#Step 1: Train the model

Open Teachable Machine, choose Image Project, then Standard image model.

  1. Rename Class 1 to Rock and Class 2 to Paper. Click Add a class twice and name the new cards Scissors and Nothing.
  2. For each gesture, click Webcam, then press and hold Hold to Record while moving your hand around the frame: closer, farther, tilted. Aim for about 80 samples per class.
  3. For Nothing, record the empty background for about the same number of samples.
  4. Click Train Model and stay on the tab until it says Model Trained.

The Nothing class matters here. Without it, the model has to call an empty frame Rock, Paper, or Scissors, and your stress test would be full of nonsense answers before it even starts.

#Step 2: Read Teachable Machine's own report, and doubt it

Under the Training card, click Advanced, then Under the hood. Click Calculate accuracy per class and Calculate confusion matrix.

You'll probably see numbers at or near 100%. Teachable Machine got them by holding back 15% of your samples as test samples, never training on them, and checking the model on them afterwards. That's a fair method, with one catch. Your held-back samples were recorded in the same seconds, the same light, and with the same hand as the training samples. They're near-copies. The test answers "did it learn my recordings?", not "will it work tomorrow, for someone else?"

So you'll write a harder test.

#Step 3: Plan the stress test

Pick four conditions, each one a change the model might meet in real use:

Condition What changes
Same desk Nothing. This is your baseline.
Dim light Turn off the main light, keep a lamp on
New background Move to a different room or hold a patterned shirt behind your hand
Friend's hand Someone else makes the gestures: different size, skin tone, rings, nails

For each condition, show each gesture three times: 4 × 3 × 3 = 36 tests. Before each one, say what you expect. Then hold the gesture still for two seconds and write down the top class and its percentage.

⚠️ Watch out

Ask before you put someone else's hand in front of your camera, and tell them the samples stay in your browser unless you save. You don't need their face in the frame at all. Module 6 covers consent properly; for now, ask, explain, and keep faces out.

#Step 4: Write the log

Here's one tester's log. Each line is one condition and one gesture, followed by the three results.

75%. Down from Teachable Machine's 100%, and that's a single number. The next three charts open it up. If you're using Colab, paste these cells into a notebook and replace the log with your own lines; if not, tally your results on paper and use the charts to see what your tallies mean.

#Step 5: Draw the confusion matrix

Each row is what you showed the model; each column is what it said. Correct answers sit on the diagonal from top left.

The Paper column is the story. Six of the nine mistakes are the model saying Paper when it wasn't. Scissors is the worst-recognized gesture (7 of 12), and most of its errors become Paper, which makes sense: two spread fingers in poor light look a lot like an open hand. When one column soaks up the mistakes, the model has learned a "default" answer it falls back on when unsure.

#Step 6: Split accuracy by condition

The model is perfect for the person who trained it and wrong almost half the time for the next person. This is Gender Shades at kitchen-table scale: the overall number (75%) describes nobody. It's too low for you and too high for your friend.

#Step 7: Choose a "not sure" threshold

A game can refuse to answer: if the top class is below some percentage, say "Not sure, try again." Where should that line go? Plot the confidence of every right answer and every wrong one:

At 80%, five of the nine mistakes become a harmless "not sure". That's a real improvement. But look at the other four orange dots, sitting at 81% to 93%. They're all from the friend's hand, and the threshold can't touch them: the model is confidently wrong.

Now read the last printed line. Of the five right answers the threshold throws away, four belong to the friend. So the person the model already serves worst also gets asked to "try again" most. A threshold is a fair-looking rule that can still land unevenly. Raising it to 95% would catch every mistake and reject most of your friend's correct answers too.

#Step 8: Fix the data, retrain, retest

The charts point at the cause: the model only ever saw one hand in one light. With permission, record samples from two more people and in dim light, add them to the same classes, and click Train Model again. Then rerun all 36 tests with the same rules.

The friend's-hand bar jumped the most, because that's where the training data was thinnest. You didn't change a single setting. You changed who was in the data, which is usually where fairness problems begin and where they're fixed.

One honest caveat: nine tests per condition is a small sample. A jump from 5 to 8 right answers is encouraging, not proof. A real product team would run hundreds of tests per group.

#The finished stress test

Your finished work is three things: the log (36 lines), the charts or hand tallies, and the report card at the top of this lesson filled in with your numbers. Write the last line ("Use it for") yourself. It's a judgement, and it's the most important line on the card.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Teachable Machine reported 100% test accuracy, but your stress test found 75%. Why the gap?

  • Its method is fine. The issue is which samples it tested on.

  • Held-back near-copies of training pictures can't reveal what happens with a new hand or room.

  • There's no fixed penalty. The gap depends on how different real use is from your recordings.

Show answer

B. Held-back near-copies of training pictures can't reveal what happens with a new hand or room.

2A threshold of 80% caught 5 of 9 mistakes. Why didn't it catch the other 4?

  • Then they'd have been caught. Check the dot plot: they sit to the right of the line.

  • A threshold filters uncertain answers. It can't help when the model is sure and wrong.

  • It applies to every test. It just can't separate confident mistakes from confident right answers.

Show answer

B. A threshold filters uncertain answers. It can't help when the model is sure and wrong.

3Which single change did the most to fix the worst condition?

  • That would hide mistakes by refusing most of the friend's answers, right or wrong.

  • More passes over one person's hand teach it that hand more thoroughly, not other hands.

  • The errors came from missing variety in the data, so adding that variety is the direct fix.

Show answer

C. The errors came from missing variety in the data, so adding that variety is the direct fix.

Key takeaways

  • Built-in test accuracy only shows how a model handles pictures like its training pictures. Real use needs a stress test.
  • Plan tests by condition, predict before each one, and log the top class and its confidence.
  • A confusion matrix shows which mistakes happen; one column soaking up errors means the model has a fallback answer.
  • Split accuracy by condition or group. The average can describe nobody.
  • A threshold catches uncertain mistakes but not confident ones, and its "try again" cost can fall hardest on the group already served worst.

#Extend it

  • Add a fifth condition you think will be hard (gloves, a phone screen showing a hand, a younger sibling's hand) and predict its bar before testing.
  • Try thresholds of 70%, 80%, and 90% and fill in a small table: mistakes caught, right answers lost, and whose they were.
  • Build a two-class "thumbs up / thumbs down" model and see whether the same conditions break it in the same way.

#Further reading

  • Teachable Machine FAQ (opens in a new tab): the "I trained a model... what now?" section suggests more ways to stress-test, including changing backgrounds, microphones, and voices.
  • Fairness in Google's Machine Learning Crash Course (opens in a new tab): how professionals check model results across groups.
  • Thresholds and the confusion matrix (opens in a new tab): a second look at Step 7 with an interactive slider.

m5-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Label a mistake as a false positive or a false negative in a real setting.
  • Fill in a confusion matrix from a description and compute accuracy from it.
  • Choose a threshold by weighing the cost of each kind of mistake.
  • Explain why a positive result for a rare condition is often a false alarm.
  • Split accuracy by group and name the likely source of a bias.

These are thinking problems, not coding problems. Write your answer in a sentence or two before opening the solution. Some solutions include a short Python cell that checks the arithmetic and draws a chart; you can read the chart without reading the code.

#Warm-up: what does 51% mean?

A Cat/Dog model in Teachable Machine shows Cat 51%, Dog 49% for a photo. What should you conclude, and what should a program using this model do?

Show solution

The model can barely tell. 51 to 49 is a near tie, so the honest reading is "unsure", not "cat". It also doesn't mean there's a 51% chance of a cat; the bars just split 100 points between the two answers it knows. A careful program would treat anything this close as "not sure" and ask for another photo, or a person, instead of acting on it.

#Exercise 1: Name the mistake

For each case, say whether it's a false positive or a false negative. Decide first what "positive" means in that system.

  1. A spam filter sends your coach's practice-time email to spam.
  2. An airport scanner lets a bag with a knife through.
  3. Face unlock opens your phone for your brother.
  4. A plagiarism checker flags an essay you wrote yourself.
  5. A smoke alarm stays silent while a pan catches fire.
Need a hint?

Ask: what is the system trying to detect? That's "positive". A false positive is a "yes" that should have been "no"; a false negative is a "no" that should have been "yes".

Show solution
Case "Positive" means Mistake
Coach's email in spam Spam False positive
Knife missed Dangerous item False negative
Phone opens for brother "This is the owner" False positive
Original essay flagged Copied work False positive
Silent smoke alarm Fire False negative

Number 3 trips people up. The phone isn't detecting "a stranger"; it's detecting "the owner", and it said yes to someone who isn't.

#Exercise 2: Build a confusion matrix from a story

A plant app checks 200 leaf photos. 40 of the leaves really are diseased. The app flags 50 leaves as diseased, and 32 of those really are. Fill in the four cells, then answer: what is the accuracy? What share of diseased leaves did it catch? What share of its flags were right?

Need a hint?

Start with the cell you're given (32 flagged and diseased). The other three come from subtraction: 40 diseased in total, 50 flags in total, 200 leaves in total.

Show solution

Accuracy is 87%, which sounds good. But the app missed 1 in 5 diseased leaves, and more than a third of its warnings were false alarms. The last two numbers have names you'll meet later: the share caught is recall and the share of flags that are right is precision. Accuracy alone hides both.

#Exercise 3: Pick the threshold

Each system gives a score from 0 to 1 and acts when the score is above a threshold. For each, would you choose low (around 0.2), middle (0.5), or high (around 0.9)? Give one sentence of reasoning.

  1. A school email spam filter.
  2. A smartwatch fall detector that automatically texts a family member.
  3. A party game that shouts "Dog!" when a dog walks past the camera.
Need a hint?

For each one, write down what a false positive costs and what a false negative costs, and who pays each cost.

Show solution
  1. High. A false positive hides a real message, maybe an urgent one. A false negative is one more junk email. Lost real email is the worse mistake.
  2. Low. A missed fall can leave someone on the floor for hours. A false alarm means an "Are you okay?" text and a mildly annoyed reply. Many fall detectors also add a short countdown the wearer can cancel, which keeps the threshold low while cutting the false alarms.
  3. Middle, or whatever is most fun. Neither mistake hurts anyone. Not every system needs careful tuning, and recognising that is part of good judgement.

#Exercise 4: The rare-disease puzzle

A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test catches 99% of people who have it, and wrongly says "positive" for 5% of healthy people. Your friend tests positive. Roughly what is the chance they actually have the disease: 99%, 50%, or about 2%?

Need a hint?

Imagine 100,000 people. How many have the disease, and how many of those test positive? How many are healthy, and how many of those test positive? Your friend is somewhere in the combined positive pile.

Show solution

About 2%. The test is good, but healthy people outnumber sick people 999 to 1, so even a small false-positive rate produces far more false alarms than true cases. This is why a positive screening result leads to a second, different test rather than a diagnosis. The same trap catches any detector hunting for something rare: cheating, fraud, a particular face in a crowd.

#Exercise 5: Accuracy by group

A homework-helper app recognises spoken questions. Its makers tested 500 recordings and report "90% accurate". Here's the breakdown:

Group Recordings Understood correctly
Adults, native English speakers 300 291
Teens 120 108
Children under 10 50 33
Adults learning English 30 18

Compute each group's accuracy. Who is the app for, according to its name, and how well does it serve them?

Need a hint?

Divide the second column by the first for each row. Then compare the groups the app was tested on most with the groups it's meant to help.

Show solution

A homework helper is mostly for students, yet children under 10 get two-thirds of their questions understood and English learners only 60%. The average is high because 300 of the 500 test recordings came from the group it serves best. Real speech systems have shown this pattern: a 2020 study by Koenecke and colleagues found that speech-to-text services from five large companies made almost twice as many errors for Black speakers as for white speakers.

#Exercise 6: Where did the bias come from?

Crash Course AI lists five sources of bias: data that reflects existing biases, unbalanced classes, data that doesn't capture what you actually care about, feedback loops, and deliberately bad data. Match each real case to one source.

  1. Amazon built an experimental résumé-screening model trained on résumés sent to the company over ten years, most of them from men. Reuters reported in 2018 that it learned to downgrade résumés containing the word "women's", and the company dropped it.
  2. A hospital program estimated how sick patients were from how much money had been spent on their care. Because less had historically been spent on Black patients with the same needs, it underrated how sick they were (Obermeyer and colleagues, Science, 2019).
  3. Microsoft's Tay chatbot (2016) learned from conversations on Twitter. Users flooded it with offensive messages, and within a day it was repeating them.
  4. A skin-condition app is trained on photos that are mostly of light skin.
  5. Police are sent where past arrests were recorded; more police there record more arrests; next year's model sends even more police there.
Need a hint?

For each, ask: was the data an accurate record of an unfair past, a lopsided sample, the wrong measurement, poisoned on purpose, or shaped by the model's own decisions?

Show solution
  1. Data that reflects existing biases. The records were accurate, but they recorded a male-dominated industry, so the model learned to prefer what had been preferred.
  2. Data that doesn't capture what you care about. Spending was used as a stand-in for need, and the two weren't the same for every group.
  3. Deliberately bad data. People fed it harmful examples on purpose.
  4. Unbalanced classes. Too few examples of darker skin, the same problem Gender Shades found in face datasets.
  5. Feedback loop. The model's own output decides where the next data comes from, so its first guess keeps confirming itself.

Cases can mix sources. That's fine, as long as you can explain the main one.

#Challenge: Write a fairness test plan

Your school library is thinking about a voice-controlled kiosk that answers "Where is this book?" Before anyone buys it, write a one-page test plan. Include: which groups of users to test, how many recordings per group, which conditions (noise, distance), what you'll measure, the biggest gap between groups you'd accept, and what happens when the kiosk isn't sure.

Show solution

A strong plan looks something like this. Yours can differ in the details, as long as every choice has a reason.

The two lines people forget are the last two: measuring who gets the "not sure" fallback (you saw in the build-along that it can fall unevenly), and testing again after updates, because a model that passed once can change.
