m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain the difference between a model learning patterns and a model memorizing examples.
  • Show why a dataset with no names can still identify people.
  • List what makes consent real: informed, specific, voluntary, and possible to withdraw.
  • Describe both sides of the face recognition debate with real cases.
  • State the basic COPPA rule for collecting data from children under 13 in the US.

In August 2006, AOL published about 20 million search queries so researchers could study them. To protect its users, it replaced each person's name with a number. Within days, New York Times reporters read the searches of user No. 4417749 (landscapers in Lilburn, Georgia; people with the surname Arnold; a dog that pees on everything) and knocked on the door of Thelma Arnold, a 62-year-old widow in Lilburn. She confirmed the searches were hers.

Nobody at AOL typed her name into that file. Her searches were her name. Machine learning makes this problem bigger, because models are trained on enormous piles of exactly this kind of data.

#Learning patterns versus memorizing examples

When you train a Teachable Machine model, the result isn't a folder of your photos. Its FAQ describes the uploaded model as "the mathematical program that predicts which class you're showing it", and the samples themselves are never published with it. A model is millions of numbers tuned to separate your classes.

But "it's just numbers" doesn't mean "it remembers nothing." Models can memorize: store a specific training example closely enough to reproduce it. Memorization is most likely for examples that are rare, unusual, or repeated many times, and bigger models memorize more.

In 2021, Nicholas Carlini and researchers from Google, OpenAI, Apple, and several universities showed this on GPT-2, a language model trained on text from the web. By asking it to write freely and then searching its outputs for oddly specific text, they pulled out hundreds of passages copied word for word from its training data. One was a real person's full name, email address, phone number, and home address.

The rule of thumb that follows: anything in the training data might come back out. If you wouldn't post it publicly, think hard before training on it.

#"We removed the names" is not anonymous

Information that isn't a name but can combine to point at one person is called a quasi-identifier: ZIP code, birth date, gender, school, job title, even a list of movies you rated.

  • In 1997, Latanya Sweeney found the hospital records of Massachusetts governor William Weld in a "de-identified" state health dataset. She matched his ZIP code, gender, and birth date against a voter list she bought for $20. Using 1990 census data, she later estimated that 87% of Americans could likely be singled out by those three facts alone.
  • In 2008, Arvind Narayanan and Vitaly Shmatikov took the "anonymous" movie ratings Netflix had released for a prize contest and linked some of them to people's public reviews on IMDb, connecting those public profiles to private viewing histories.

Here's why it works. The chart builds a made-up town of 30,000 people and counts how many become the only person matching what you know, as you learn one more fact at a time:

The first three facts barely matter: thousands of people share a ZIP code and gender, and dozens share a birth year too. Then the full birth date arrives and most of the town becomes unique. That cliff is the danger. Each column looks harmless on its own; the combination is a fingerprint.

The defences are real but limited: generalize (birth year instead of birth date, a region instead of a ZIP code), aggregate (publish counts, not rows), or add carefully measured random noise, a method called differential privacy that the US Census Bureau used for the 2020 census. All of them trade some usefulness for privacy.

#Consent that means something

Consent is real when it is:

  • Informed: people know what's collected, why, who sees it, and how long it's kept.
  • Specific: it covers a stated purpose. "Data that may be useful later" isn't a purpose.
  • Voluntary: saying no doesn't cost them something they need, and there's an equal alternative.
  • Revocable: they can change their mind, and their data actually gets deleted.

"It was public" is not consent for every use. Clearview AI collected billions of photos from public websites and social media (over 30 billion, according to the Dutch data protection authority) to build a face search engine sold mainly to police. Nobody in those photos agreed to that. Regulators in France, Italy, and Greece each fined the company €20 million, the UK fined it £7.5 million in 2022, and the Netherlands fined it €30.5 million in 2024.

#Why face recognition is so disputed

Faces are unlike passwords: you can't change yours, and a camera can capture it from across a street without you knowing. That's why the same technology gets very different reactions depending on how it's used.

Unlocking your own phone compares your face to one stored template, on a device you own, after you chose to set it up. Scanning a crowd compares everyone who walks past against a database, and none of them chose anything.

The case against crowd scanning is concrete. In January 2020, Robert Williams was arrested at his home in Michigan, in front of his daughters, because face recognition software matched him to blurry shoplifting footage. It wasn't him. Gender Shades had already shown these systems err more on darker-skinned faces. San Francisco banned city agencies from using face recognition in 2019. In June 2020, IBM said it would stop offering general-purpose face recognition, Amazon paused police use of its Rekognition product, and Microsoft said it wouldn't sell to US police without a federal law.

The case for some uses is concrete too: finding missing children, identifying victims after disasters, unlocking a phone without typing a code. Most of the serious argument isn't "faces: yes or no" but who uses it, on whom, with whose consent, and with what checks when it's wrong.

#Kids' data and COPPA

In the US, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) applies to websites, apps, and online services aimed at children under 13, and to any service that knows it's collecting from under-13s. The basics:

  • Get verifiable parental consent before collecting a child's personal information. A checkbox the child ticks doesn't count.
  • "Personal information" includes a photo, video, or audio file containing a child's image or voice, as well as names, contact details, and location.
  • Parents can review their child's data and have it deleted. Keep it only as long as needed.

The Federal Trade Commission enforces COPPA. In 2019, Google and YouTube paid $170 million to settle claims that YouTube collected data from children watching kid-directed channels without parental consent. Updated COPPA rules took effect in June 2025, adding requirements such as separate parental consent before sharing kids' data with third parties like advertisers, and a written policy on how long data is kept.

COPPA stops at 13, but good practice doesn't. Teens' data is still personal, schools have their own rules (FERPA in the US), and Europe's GDPR sets an age of digital consent between 13 and 16 depending on the country. None of this is legal advice; it's the minimum to know before you build anything that records people.

⚠️ Watch out

Three privacy mistakes beginners make

  1. "It's public, so it's fine to use." Public means visible, not "agreed to any purpose." Ask whether the people would expect your use.
  2. "We deleted the names, so it's anonymous." Check for combinations of quasi-identifiers. If three or four columns together point at one person, it isn't anonymous.
  3. "We'll delete it later." Later never comes without a date. Write the deletion date down when you collect the data.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A school shares a spreadsheet of student survey answers with names removed but keeps grade, homeroom, gender, and birthday. What's the main risk?

  • Names aren't the only identifiers. Homeroom plus birthday probably points at one student.

  • These are quasi-identifiers. In a homeroom of 30, very few students share a gender and a birthday.

  • True of any file, but the specific problem here is that the "anonymous" data isn't anonymous.

Show answer

B. These are quasi-identifiers. In a homeroom of 30, very few students share a gender and a birthday.

2Your Teachable Machine model was trained on photos of your face. You click Upload my model. What gets published?

  • The FAQ says the samples you trained on are not published with the model.

  • The photos stay private, yet the model itself carries information about you, so think before sharing it.

  • Training runs in the browser, but uploading publishes the model to Google's servers at a shareable link.

Show answer

B. The photos stay private, yet the model itself carries information about you, so think before sharing it.

3Which of these is the strongest example of real consent?

  • Not voluntary if you need to enter, and not specific about use or retention.

  • "Future projects" isn't a specific purpose, and nothing says how long the data is kept.

  • It's informed, specific, voluntary, and revocable.

Show answer

C. It's informed, specific, voluntary, and revocable.

4A homework app for 9-year-olds records children reading aloud. Under COPPA, what must it do before recording?

  • Children under 13 can't give this consent themselves.

  • Voice recordings of a child are personal information, so a parent must agree first, in a way that confirms they really are the parent.

  • COPPA explicitly covers audio files that contain a child's voice.

Show answer

B. Voice recordings of a child are personal information, so a parent must agree first, in a way that confirms they really are the parent.

Key takeaways

  • Models learn patterns but can also memorize rare or repeated examples, so anything in training data might come back out.
  • Removing names rarely anonymizes data. Combinations like ZIP, gender, and birth date single out most people.
  • Real consent is informed, specific, voluntary, and revocable. "Public" and "useful later" don't qualify.
  • Face recognition is disputed because faces can't be changed and can be captured without consent; the key questions are who uses it, on whom, and with what checks.
  • COPPA requires verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information, including photos and voice, from children under 13.

#Further reading

  • Why Some Models Leak Data (opens in a new tab): an interactive essay from Google's PAIR team that shows memorization happening in a small model.
  • Simple Demographics Often Identify People Uniquely (opens in a new tab): Latanya Sweeney's own summary of the 87% finding, with more combinations to compare.
  • Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (opens in a new tab): a readable overview of COPPA's rules, history, and major enforcement cases.

m6-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write a one-sentence purpose that limits what data a project may collect.
  • Inventory every piece of data a Teachable Machine project creates, and where each one goes.
  • Choose the least sensitive data that still does the job.
  • Write a consent request that is informed, specific, voluntary, and revocable.
  • Set retention and deletion rules, and test the plan against "what if" cases.

Here's the pitch from your school's robotics club: "Let's put a laptop by the door that recognizes members' faces and says hi by name. And let's record everyone's voice too, since we might do a voice project later."

It's a fun idea, and every part of that second sentence is a privacy problem. Nobody has said why voices are needed, how long they'll be kept, or what happens if someone says no. You're going to turn the pitch into a plan the club could actually show to members and their parents.

The finished plan has six parts, and each step below builds one of them:

#Step 1: Write the purpose in one sentence

A purpose is a promise about what the data is for. Everything not covered by the purpose doesn't get collected. Write it with the decision the system makes:

Notice what this sentence already rules out. Taking attendance, tracking who's late, and "a voice project later" are all different purposes. If the club wants them, each needs its own plan and its own consent. The voice recordings are already gone: nothing in the purpose needs them.

#Step 2: List every piece of data

Go through the original pitch and list everything the project would create. Include things that don't feel like data:

Data Why it would exist Sensitive?
Face photos of each member Training samples, one class per person Yes: biometric, can't be changed
Members' names They'd be the class names Yes, once linked to faces
Voice clips "Might be useful later" Yes, and no purpose
The trained model Result of training Yes: it can pick out those faces
Faces of passers-by The camera sees the hallway Yes, and they never agreed

Two rows surprise most people. The class names turn a pile of photos into "this face is Priya." And the camera at the door sees everyone walking past, not just members.

#Step 3: Map where the data goes

Teachable Machine's FAQ is clear about where things live, so you can draw it exactly:

Solid arrows happen every time. Dotted arrows only happen if someone clicks that option. Close the tab without clicking any of them and nothing is kept anywhere. The plan's job is to decide which dotted arrows the club is allowed to use.

For this project the answer is: one place to save the project, and never Upload my model. A face model at a public link is a tool anyone with the link can use to recognize your members.

#Step 4: Choose the least data that works

The purpose is "show a welcome message." Does that need to know who someone is? Compare the options:

Option What it records Problems
Face recognition by name Every member's face, plus names Biometric data; visitors who aren't members get forced into a member's name (no "Nothing" class covers every stranger); younger members need parent consent
Wave to be greeted Hands waving at chest height, plus an empty-doorway class Very little; point the camera so faces aren't in frame
Name badge or tapping your name on a screen Nothing recorded Not machine learning at all, but works perfectly

Remember the forced-choice problem from Module 5: a model with one class per member has to pick some member for every face it sees. A friend dropping by gets greeted as "Hi, Marcus!" with 90% confidence. That's a privacy problem (it's guessing identities) and a fairness problem (it'll be wrong more for faces unlike the training set).

The club picks wave to be greeted: a two-class image model, Wave and Nothing, with a generic "Welcome to Robotics Club!" It keeps the fun and drops the faces.

📝 Note

Choosing less data isn't giving up. The best privacy protection is data you never collected: it can't leak, be stolen, or be used for something else later.

#Step 5: Write the consent request

Even waving hands are recordings of people, so the volunteers who train the model should agree first. A good request answers five questions in plain words: what, why, who sees it, how long, and how to say no.

The last line borrows COPPA's idea. COPPA is a law for online services, not a club laptop, but its principle (a parent agrees for children under 13) is good practice for any project. Many schools require parent permission for older students too, so check your school's rules.

#Step 6: Decide how data is kept and deleted

Withdrawal is easy to promise and hard to do. Teachable Machine mixes everyone's samples in one class, so deleting "Sam's waves" later is messy. Plan for it now:

  1. Each volunteer records on a phone or the laptop camera, and their photos go into their own folder named with a number, not their name.
  2. Build the project by clicking Upload on the Wave card and choosing photos from those folders.
  3. If someone withdraws: delete their folder, start a new project, upload the remaining folders, and click Train Model again.
  4. Keep one copy of the project with Download project as file in the club folder. Don't also save it to Drive; two copies means two places to forget.
  5. On the deletion date, delete the folders and the project file, and write down that you did.

#Step 7: Test the plan with "what if" questions

A plan is only good if it survives awkward situations. Answer each in one line:

What if... Answer in the plan
A member withdraws in March? Delete their folder, rebuild, retrain that week.
A visitor's face appears in the camera? Nothing is recorded while the greeter runs, the model only knows Wave and Nothing, and the camera points below face height.
Someone wants to add voices later? New purpose, new plan, new consent. Not covered by this one.
The laptop is shared with another club? Project file stays in a folder only club officers can open.
Someone asks "is my data in the model?" The model contains patterns from the volunteers' hand photos, not the photos themselves; withdrawing removes them at the next retrain.

#The finished plan

That's the whole build. It fits on a page, every line has a reason, and a parent could read it in two minutes.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why did the plan drop the voice recordings in Step 1, before anyone discussed risks?

  • A purpose limits collection. "Might be useful later" isn't a purpose, so the data doesn't get collected.

  • It isn't illegal in general. It just needs a reason and consent, and this project had neither.

  • It can (Audio Project). The problem was purpose, not the tool.

Show answer

A. A purpose limits collection. "Might be useful later" isn't a purpose, so the data doesn't get collected.

2Why is face recognition by name a poor fit for a door greeter, even with every member's consent?

  • An image model can learn faces. The problem is what happens with faces it wasn't trained on.

  • With one class per member, every face must get some member's name, often with high confidence.

  • Training time is similar. The issues are consent, identity guesses, and data that can't be changed.

Show answer

B. With one class per member, every face must get some member's name, often with high confidence.

3Why does the plan store each volunteer's photos in a separate numbered folder?

  • It doesn't. The folders are for the club's benefit, not the tool's.

  • Once samples are mixed in a class, removing one person's is hard. Separate folders make withdrawal real.

  • Folder structure doesn't change what the model learns.

Show answer

B. Once samples are mixed in a class, removing one person's is hard. Separate folders make withdrawal real.

Key takeaways

  • Start with a one-sentence purpose. Data the purpose doesn't need doesn't get collected.
  • Inventory everything, including class names, the trained model, and people the camera sees by accident.
  • Map where data can go; in Teachable Machine, samples leave the tab only if you save to Drive or download the project.
  • Choose the least sensitive data that does the job. Often that removes faces entirely.
  • Consent answers what, why, who, how long, and how to say no, with an equal alternative and a real way to withdraw.

#Extend it

  • Write a data plan for a project you actually want to build, using the seven-line format above.
  • Swap roles: give your plan to a friend and have them play a worried parent. Every question they ask that the plan doesn't answer is a missing line.
  • Find the privacy policy of an app you use. Which of the five consent questions (what, why, who, how long, how to say no) does it answer clearly?

What you'll learn

  • Tell personal and sensitive data apart from data that identifies no one.
  • Rewrite a vague consent request so it is informed, specific, voluntary, and revocable.
  • Test a table for anonymity by counting how many people share each combination of details.
  • Decide whether COPPA applies to an app, and what it requires.
  • Weigh the benefits and risks of a face recognition proposal and make a recommendation.

There's rarely one perfect answer to a privacy question, but there are clearly better and worse ones. Write yours down first, then compare it with the model answer. If your reasoning is different but sound, that counts.

#Warm-up: which of these is about a person?

  1. "41 students in our grade like pizza best."
  2. A photo of the back of your head, taken in your front yard.
  3. Your student ID number.
  4. "The cafeteria ran out of milk on Tuesday."
Show solution

Numbers 2 and 3 are personal information. The photo shows your house, which reveals where you live, even without your face. A student ID points at exactly one student in the school's records. Number 1 is a count (an aggregate) and number 4 is about the cafeteria, so neither identifies anyone, as long as the group is big enough that a count can't be traced back to one person.

#Exercise 1: Sort the data

Put each item into not personal, personal, or sensitive (personal data that could cause real harm if exposed, such as health, biometrics, exact location, or anything about a child):

  • The class average on last week's quiz
  • A one-second voice clip of you saying "hello"
  • Your home address
  • A smartwatch log of your heart rate every minute
  • Your gamer tag
  • Today's weather at school
Need a hint?

Ask two questions: does this point to one person, and if it leaked, could it hurt them? A gamer tag points to someone even though it isn't their legal name.

Show solution
Item Category Why
Class average Not personal An aggregate of many students (unless the class has two people in it)
Voice clip Sensitive A voice is biometric; it can identify you and can be used to clone your voice
Home address Sensitive Exact location, which matters for safety
Heart-rate log Sensitive Health data; it can also reveal sleep, stress, and when you're home
Gamer tag Personal It points to one person and can be linked to their other accounts
Weather Not personal Not about anyone

#Exercise 2: Rewrite a bad consent request

A photo-filter app shows this when it first opens:

List what's wrong, then rewrite it.

Need a hint?

Check it against the five questions from the build-along: what, why, who sees it, how long, and how to say no. How many does it answer?

Show solution

It answers almost none. "Using the app" isn't a choice to share photos, "improve our products" and "other business purposes" could mean anything (including training a face model or selling data), it doesn't say who sees the photos or for how long, and there's no way to say no without losing the app.

The key changes: a real choice with equal buttons, one specific purpose, named limits on who sees it and how long, and a working way to change your mind.

#Exercise 3: Is this survey anonymous?

A school publishes a wellbeing survey with names removed. Each row is one student: grade, homeroom, gender, birth month, and whether they said they feel stressed. Is it anonymous? If not, which columns would you remove or blur, and does that fully fix it?

Need a hint?

Count how many students share each combination of grade, homeroom, gender, and birth month. Any combination with exactly one student points at that student. Then try keeping fewer columns and count again.

Show solution

With all four columns, every one of the 12 students is alone in their group: anyone who knows a classmate's grade, homeroom, and birth month can read their answer. Dropping homeroom and birth month puts every student in a group of at least 3. Privacy researchers call this k-anonymity with k = 3.

But look at the printed table. All three grade-10 girls said yes. The table is now "3-anonymous", yet anyone who knows a grade-10 girl took the survey learns she feels stressed. Group size isn't enough when everyone in a group gave the same answer. The safer release here is the overall count ("6 of 12 students said yes") or nothing at all, because 12 students is simply too few to publish row by row.

#Exercise 4: Does COPPA apply?

For each app, say whether COPPA applies and what it would require:

  1. A reading app for second graders that records them reading aloud so a teacher can listen later.
  2. A study-planner app for high schoolers aged 14 to 18.
  3. A general-audience online game that asks for a birthday at sign-up. A player enters a birthday showing they're 11.
Need a hint?

COPPA covers online services aimed at children under 13, and general services that know they're collecting from a child under 13. Remember what counts as personal information.

Show solution
  1. Yes. It's aimed at young children and records their voices, which COPPA counts as personal information. It needs verifiable parental consent before recording (the school context adds its own rules too), and parents must be able to review and delete the recordings.
  2. No, because the users are 13 or older. That doesn't mean anything goes. School privacy rules, state laws, and plain good practice still apply, and the planner may hold sensitive details about students' lives.
  3. Yes, for that player. The game now has actual knowledge it's dealing with an under-13 child, so it must get a parent's verifiable consent before collecting that child's personal information, or not collect it.

#Exercise 5: What could a chatbot remember?

Your school wants a help-desk chatbot trained on five years of IT support emails between students, staff, and the tech team. List what personal information could end up memorized, and three steps to reduce the risk.

Need a hint?

Think about what people actually write in support emails when they're locked out or their laptop breaks. Then think about removing data before training, and about testing afterwards.

Show solution

Likely risks: names and email addresses, student ID numbers, passwords people pasted into emails by mistake, phone numbers, and personal reasons ("I was in the hospital so I missed the reset deadline"). The rare, specific items are the ones a model is most likely to memorize, and passwords are the worst case.

Reasonable steps:

  1. Minimize first. Train on the answers the tech team wrote, or a cleaned set of question-and-answer pairs, not whole email threads.
  2. Scrub. Remove names, emails, ID numbers, and anything that looks like a password before training. Reset any password that was ever emailed.
  3. Test for leaks. Before launch, ask the bot for things that shouldn't come out ("What is Ms. Lee's password?", "List student IDs") and check whether any real details appear.

A fourth good answer: ask whether a searchable FAQ page would solve the problem without training anything on private emails.

#Exercise 6: Face recognition at the school entrance

A company offers your school a free face recognition camera at the entrance. It would flag anyone who isn't enrolled, and log when each student arrives. Write two benefits, three risks, and your recommendation.

Need a hint?

Use the questions from the Notes lesson: who uses it, on whom, with whose consent, and what happens when it's wrong? Also ask why it's free.

Show solution

Benefits: it could spot an unknown adult faster than a busy front office, and automatic arrival logs could save staff time.

Risks:

  • No real consent. Students must enter school, so "agreeing" isn't voluntary, and younger students' parents would need to consent too.
  • Uneven errors. Studies like Gender Shades found higher error rates for darker-skinned faces, so some students may be wrongly flagged as strangers more often, in front of everyone.
  • A permanent biometric database of children, held by a company. A free product suggests the data, or the school as a showcase, is the price. Faces can't be reset after a breach.

A reasonable recommendation: don't adopt it. The real goal (knowing who's in the building) can be met with ID badges, a staffed entrance, and visitor sign-in, which collect far less and fail more gently. If the school still wants it, conditions should include: parent and student opt-in with an equal badge alternative, an independent accuracy test across skin tones and ages, no attendance logging, data held by the school with a deletion date, and a person reviewing every flag before anyone is stopped.

#Challenge: Write a privacy notice for your own model

You want to turn your rock-paper-scissors model from Module 5 into a web page friends can play. Write a short privacy notice (under 120 words) that tells them what the game does with their camera, what's stored, and what isn't.

Show solution

Check every sentence against what really happens. A common way to build the page is to click Upload my model and paste Teachable Machine's JavaScript code snippet into a web page. That publishes the model at a link but not the training photos, and the snippet runs the model in the player's browser. If you build it differently, rewrite the notice to match: a privacy notice that's wrong is worse than none.

What you'll learn

  • Explain why a language model can produce a fluent, confident, false answer.
  • Describe three real deepfake incidents and why spotting glitches by eye isn't enough.
  • Check a suspicious image, video, or quote with the SIFT method and the right tools.
  • Use five questions (task, data, stakes, errors, alternatives) to decide whether AI fits a problem.

In February 2023, Google posted a short ad for its new chatbot, Bard. Someone asked what to tell a 9-year-old about the James Webb Space Telescope, and Bard answered with three facts. One of them said the telescope took the very first pictures of a planet outside our solar system. It didn't: the first such image came in 2004, from the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope in Chile. Astronomers pointed it out on social media, Reuters reported it, and Alphabet lost roughly $100 billion in market value the day the story spread.

The answer was confident, well written, and wrong. Nothing about its tone gave the mistake away. That's the problem this lesson is about.

#Why chatbots make things up

A large language model is trained to do one thing: given some text, predict what word comes next. It learns this from an enormous amount of writing. When you ask it a question, it writes an answer one word at a time, each time choosing a likely next word.

"Likely" means likely to appear in text like this, not true. Most of the time those overlap, which is why chatbots are so useful. When they don't overlap, you get a hallucination: a fluent answer with invented facts, quotes, or sources. The right answer and the wrong one come out of exactly the same process, in the same confident voice.

Here's a toy version. It isn't how Bard works inside, but it shows the core idea: the toy picks whichever word followed "taken by" most often in its training text.

The true answer, VLT, was in the training text, but rarely. In news coverage, the James Webb telescope is mentioned far more often alongside exoplanet pictures, so it wins. Real models are vastly more sophisticated, and they're also trained to be helpful and to admit uncertainty, but they can still produce the popular-sounding answer over the correct one.

Two real cases show what this costs:

  • Fake court cases (2023). Two New York lawyers filed a brief in Mata v. Avianca that cited earlier court decisions found with ChatGPT. The judge wrote that six of them appeared to be "bogus judicial decisions with bogus quotes and bogus internal citations." The lawyers had even asked ChatGPT whether the cases were real, and it said yes. The judge fined them $5,000.
  • An invented refund rule (2024). Air Canada's website chatbot told a passenger, Jake Moffatt, he could claim a bereavement discount after his flight. The airline's actual policy said otherwise. A Canadian tribunal ruled that Air Canada is responsible for everything on its own website, chatbot included, and ordered it to pay.

#Deepfakes: when seeing and hearing aren't enough

A deepfake is audio, an image, or video made or altered by AI to show someone saying or doing something they didn't. Three real incidents:

  • March 2022. During the Russian invasion, a video of Ukraine's President Zelensky telling soldiers to surrender appeared on a hacked Ukrainian news website. It was crude (the head looked pasted on), and Meta and YouTube removed it the same day.
  • January 2024. Before the New Hampshire primary, thousands of voters got a robocall in an AI-cloned voice of President Biden telling them not to vote in the primary. The Federal Communications Commission later fined the political consultant behind it $6 million.
  • Early 2024. A finance employee at the engineering firm Arup in Hong Kong joined a video call with what looked like the company's chief financial officer and several colleagues. Every one of them was a deepfake. The employee made 15 transfers totalling about US$25 million.

Notice the trend. The 2022 fake was easy to spot; the 2024 call fooled a trained professional. Advice like "look for weird hands or blinking" ages quickly, because each new generator fixes the last one's tells. Checking where something came from lasts far longer than checking how it looks.

#How to check: SIFT

The researcher Mike Caulfield's SIFT method is four moves you can make in a couple of minutes:

  1. Stop. Notice the strong feeling (shock, anger, delight) and don't share yet.
  2. Investigate the source. Who posted it? Look them up in a new tab rather than trusting their own bio.
  3. Find better coverage. Search for the claim itself. If a president really surrendered, every major news outlet would have it.
  4. Trace to the original. Find the earliest version of the image, clip, or quote, and see its full context.

For media, a few tools help with steps 3 and 4:

  • Reverse image search (Google Lens, TinEye) finds where else an image appears and often its oldest copy.
  • Content Credentials are a signed record some cameras and AI tools attach, saying how an image was made or edited. You can check a file at contentcredentials.org/verify. A credential is useful evidence; a missing one proves nothing, since most images have none.
  • A second channel. For a call or voice message asking for money or secrets, hang up and contact the person on a number you already know. That's how the Arup fraud was finally discovered, too late.

#Does AI even fit this problem?

The same skepticism applies to AI proposals. Before asking "which model?", ask whether a model belongs there at all:

  1. Task. Is there a clear right answer you could check? "Is this a cat?" has one. "Is this student trustworthy?" doesn't.
  2. Data. Is there enough data, does it represent everyone who'll be affected, and was it collected with consent?
  3. Stakes. When it's wrong, who is hurt and how badly? A bad song recommendation and a wrong school suspension are not the same.
  4. Errors. Will a person catch mistakes before they matter? Can someone affected appeal to a human?
  5. Alternatives. Would a simple rule, a form, a checklist, or a person do the job as well, more cheaply, or more fairly?

A real example: in January 2023, OpenAI released a classifier to detect AI-written text. By its own testing it caught 26% of AI-written text and wrongly flagged 9% of human-written text as AI. Run it through the questions. The task is fuzzy (people edit AI drafts and AI edits people's), the stakes are high (an accusation of cheating), errors are hard to catch (how do you prove you wrote something?), and alternatives exist (drafts, in-class writing, conversations about the work). OpenAI withdrew the tool in July 2023, citing its low accuracy.

⚠️ Watch out

Three verification mistakes

  1. Asking the chatbot if it's right. It will usually say yes, as it did for the lawyers in Mata v. Avianca. Check claims against sources outside the chatbot.
  2. "I didn't see any glitches, so it's real." Good fakes don't have visible glitches. Check the source and the original, not the pixels.
  3. Using AI because it's available. "We have an AI tool" isn't a reason. Start from the problem and the five questions.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A chatbot gives you a quote from a scientist, with a book title and page number. What should you do before using it?

  • Specific details are easy to generate. Invented citations often look exactly this precise.

  • The chatbot's confirmation comes from the same process that may have invented it.

  • Tracing a claim to its original is the only reliable check.

Show answer

C. Tracing a claim to its original is the only reliable check.

2Why did the toy model in the trace answer "Webb"?

  • It chose the most frequent continuation. Frequency in text isn't the same as truth.

  • It didn't look anything up. It only compared counts.

  • The loop compares counts, not alphabetical order.

Show answer

A. It chose the most frequent continuation. Frequency in text isn't the same as truth.

3Your aunt gets a voice message that sounds exactly like your cousin, asking for money for an emergency. What's the best first step?

  • Cloned voices can sound natural. The absence of glitches proves nothing.

  • Checking through a second channel you trust defeats almost every voice-clone scam.

  • Any payment rewards the scam. Verify before acting.

Show answer

B. Checking through a second channel you trust defeats almost every voice-clone scam.

4A school wants AI to decide which students get a scholarship. Which question from the checklist raises the biggest concern?

  • Possibly, but the deeper issue is what happens to a student when the model is wrong.

  • High-stakes decisions about people need human judgement and a real appeal, not just a score.

  • Entering data is easy. The concern is the decision itself.

Show answer

B. High-stakes decisions about people need human judgement and a real appeal, not just a score.

Key takeaways

  • Language models predict likely text, so a fluent, confident answer can be false. Check facts, quotes, and citations against outside sources.
  • Deepfakes have moved from crude videos to a convincing multi-person video call. Check where media came from, not just how it looks.
  • SIFT: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace to the original.
  • For calls asking for money or secrets, verify through a second channel you already trust.
  • Before using AI, ask about the task, data, stakes, errors, and alternatives. Sometimes the answer is "don't."

#Further reading

  • SIFT (The Four Moves) (opens in a new tab): Mike Caulfield's own short explanation of the method, with examples.
  • Content Credentials Verify (opens in a new tab): drop in an image to see whether it carries a record of how it was made.
  • Google Fact Check Explorer (opens in a new tab): search fact-checks from news organizations worldwide on a claim or image.

What you'll learn

  • Split a paragraph of AI-generated text into separate, checkable claims.
  • Decide which claims to check first by their type and the damage if they're wrong.
  • Read laterally: verify claims against original sources in other tabs, not against the answer itself.
  • Recognize an invented quote and an invented citation.
  • Apply the same process to an image that's going viral.

You asked a chatbot about the Gender Shades study from Module 5, and it gave you this. It reads well. It has numbers, a quote, and a reference. Before you put any of it in a school report, you're going to check every sentence.

📝 Note

This answer was written for this lesson to imitate a chatbot. Its mistakes are deliberate, and they're the kinds real chatbots make: a wrong detail mixed into true ones, an inflated number, an invented quote, and a reference that doesn't exist.

By the end you'll have a verification log and a corrected answer. The loop you'll follow for every claim:

#Step 1: Split the answer into claims

A claim is one statement that could be true or false on its own. Long sentences often hide two or three. Break the answer apart and number each piece:

  1. It was published in 2018.
  2. The authors were Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru, at MIT.
  3. It tested systems from Microsoft, IBM, Google, and Face++.
  4. It used 1,270 photos of politicians from six countries.
  5. The worst error rate was 34.7%, for darker-skinned women; lighter-skinned men were under 1%.
  6. Overall, the systems were about 99% accurate.
  7. Buolamwini said, "Code is never neutral, and neither are cameras."
  8. There's a 2016 paper called "Skin Tone Errors in Phone Cameras."
  9. The United States banned facial recognition in 2019.

Claim 2 is the classic hiding place. "Buolamwini and Gebru" might be right while "at MIT" is wrong, and a quick reader checks only the names.

#Step 2: Decide what to check first

You may not have time to check everything, so rank. These types of claim are most often invented, and do the most damage when wrong:

Type Claims Why it's risky
Quotes 7 Putting words in a real person's mouth
Citations 8 Easy to invent, and readers assume they're checked
Numbers 4, 5, 6 Precise-looking, easy to get slightly or badly wrong
Big real-world claims 9 A false claim about a law misleads everyone who reads it
Names, dates, places 1, 2, 3 Usually right, sometimes subtly wrong

Order for this answer: 7, 8, 6, 9, then the rest.

#Step 3: Find the original source

Don't search for the chatbot's sentences; you'll find pages that copied the same error. Search for the thing itself: the paper. Open a new tab and search Gender Shades Buolamwini Gebru 2018 paper.

You should find the paper in the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (volume 81), and the MIT Media Lab's project page. Keep both tabs open. This is lateral reading: you leave the answer and read across other sources, instead of reading the answer more closely.

#Step 4: Check the quote and the citation

Claim 7, the quote. Search for the exact words in quotation marks: "Code is never neutral, and neither are cameras". A real, memorable quote from a well-known researcher shows up in interviews, talks, or articles with a date and place. This one appears nowhere except copies of this kind of answer. Verdict: not found. An unverified quote never goes into your work, even if it sounds like something the person might say.

Claim 8, the citation. Search Google Scholar for the title. Then search for the journal. There's no paper by that title, and no journal called Journal of Machine Vision Fairness. The detail (volume 3, issue 2, pages 45 to 61) is what makes invented references convincing. Verdict: not found; fabricated. This is exactly what happened in Mata v. Avianca.

#Step 5: Check the numbers and the big claim

Open the paper's PDF. The abstract and Table 4 cover most of it.

  • Claim 5 matches: darker-skinned females had error rates "of up to 34.7%," and the paper says "the maximum error rate for lighter-skinned males is 0.8%." Supported.
  • Claim 6 doesn't. Table 4's overall accuracy is 93.7% (Microsoft), 90.0% (Face++), and 87.9% (IBM). "About 99%" isn't a rounding slip; it erases the point of the study. Wrong.
  • Claim 4: the Pilot Parliaments Benchmark has 1,270 people, members of parliament from Rwanda, Senegal, South Africa, Iceland, Finland, and Sweden. Supported.
  • Claim 9: search news coverage for facial recognition ban 2019. You'll find San Francisco banning its city agencies from using it in May 2019, followed by a few other cities. There was no national ban. Wrong.

#Step 6: Check the names, dates, and companies

  • Claim 1: the paper appears in the proceedings of the 2018 Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency. Supported.
  • Claim 2: the paper's first page lists Buolamwini at the MIT Media Lab and Gebru at Microsoft Research. Partly wrong.
  • Claim 3: the paper evaluated three products: Microsoft, IBM, and Face++. It notes that Google did not offer a public gender classifier at the time. The products also classified gender from a face, which is different from recognizing who someone is. Wrong, in two ways.

#Step 7: Write the log and the corrected answer

Here's the finished log:

And the rewrite, keeping only what survived:

Five of the original nine sentences needed fixing or removing. The corrected version is shorter, and every sentence in it can be traced to a source.

#Step 8: The same method for a viral image

Images get the same treatment, with different tools. Suppose a dramatic photo of a flooded city street is spreading after a storm, captioned with today's date and a town name.

  1. Stop. Notice that you want to share it. That's the moment to check.
  2. Reverse image search. In Chrome, right-click the image and choose to search it with Google Lens, or upload it to TinEye. Sort by oldest. If copies exist from years ago, it isn't from today's storm.
  3. Check Content Credentials at contentcredentials.org/verify. If credentials are present, they may show the camera or the AI tool that made it. If they're absent, you've learned nothing either way.
  4. Find better coverage. Do local news outlets or the town's official accounts show the same scene?
  5. Log it like the claims above: what the image claims to show, what you found, and your verdict.

🧪 Try it yourself

If you're old enough to use a chatbot under its terms (many require users to be at least 13), ask one to "summarize the Gender Shades study in one paragraph with a source." Split its answer into claims and check three of them against the paper. Did it get the overall accuracy right?

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why search for the original paper instead of searching for the chatbot's sentences?

  • They can. The problem is what you'd find.

  • Copies of an error agree with each other. Only the original can confirm or correct a claim.

  • Copyright isn't the issue. Accuracy is.

Show answer

B. Copies of an error agree with each other. Only the original can confirm or correct a claim.

2You search for a quote in every way you can think of and find it nowhere. What's the right call?

  • "Reportedly" still puts unverified words in a real person's mouth.

  • A real quote from a public figure leaves a trail. No trail means you can't use it.

  • Sounding plausible is exactly how invented quotes get through.

Show answer

B. A real quote from a public figure leaves a trail. No trail means you can't use it.

3Why were the quote and the citation checked before the publication year?

  • Rank claims by risk. Dates are usually right; references and quotes are frequently made up.

  • Order in the answer doesn't matter. Risk does.

  • It can, easily. It's just lower risk.

Show answer

A. Rank claims by risk. Dates are usually right; references and quotes are frequently made up.

Key takeaways

  • Split AI-written text into single claims before checking. Long sentences hide wrong details next to right ones.
  • Check the riskiest claims first: quotes, citations, numbers, and big real-world claims.
  • Read laterally. Verify against original sources in other tabs, never against the answer or its copies.
  • A detailed citation can be completely invented. If you can't find it, it doesn't go in your work.
  • For images: reverse search, sort by oldest, check Content Credentials, and look for trusted coverage.

#Extend it

  • Check a chatbot answer in a subject you know well, such as a sport, a game, or a book. Experts spot hallucinations faster, so notice which errors you'd have missed in an unfamiliar topic.
  • Give the original answer to a friend without telling them it's wrong. Time how long it takes them to find a problem, then show them your log.
  • Add a "confidence" column to your log: how sure are you of each verdict, and what would change your mind?

  • Gender Shades paper (opens in a new tab): the original source used in this lesson. Practice finding claims 4 to 6 in it yourself.

What you'll learn

#Warm-up: what would you check first?

"A 2021 Stanford study found that 64% of teenagers use AI chatbots every day, according to lead researcher Dr. Ana Ruiz."

Which parts of this sentence would you check, and in what order?

Show solution

This sentence was invented for the exercise, and it's built the way convincing false claims often are. Check the researcher and the study first: search for "Ana Ruiz" with "Stanford" and "chatbots". If no such person or study turns up, the rest collapses. Then check the number (64%) and the year. 2021 is also a clue: widely used chatbots like ChatGPT only launched at the end of 2022, so a 2021 study of daily teen chatbot use is unlikely to exist.

#Exercise 1: SIFT a viral post

A friend shares a screenshot of what looks like a news site headline: "Famous singer says teens should be banned from the internet." It has 50,000 shares. Write what you'd do at each SIFT step, including the exact searches you'd type.

Need a hint?

A screenshot strips away the link, so you can't click through to the source. That changes what "Investigate the source" and "Trace to the original" look like.

Show solution
  1. Stop. The headline is designed to make you angry. Don't share it yet.
  2. Investigate the source. Which news site does the screenshot claim to be from? Go to that site directly (type its address yourself) and search for the headline there.
  3. Find better coverage. Search the claim, not the screenshot: [singer's name] teens banned internet. A real statement this extreme would be covered by many outlets. Also search a fact-check site, such as Google Fact Check Explorer.
  4. Trace to the original. Look for the original interview or post where the singer supposedly said it. If every result points back to the same screenshot, treat it as unconfirmed, and say so if you reply to your friend.

Screenshots of headlines are easy to fake. When the only evidence is the screenshot, the claim isn't verified.

#Exercise 2: Plan for a voice-clone scam

A family friend gets a panicked call that sounds exactly like their son, saying he's been in a car accident and needs money sent right now. Write a three-rule plan a family could agree on before this happens.

Need a hint?

The Arup case was cracked by checking through another channel. What makes a check like that hard for a scammer to get around?

Show solution

A good plan:

  1. Hang up and call back on the number you already have saved, or call another family member who'd know.
  2. Agree on a family code word that's never posted online. Anyone asking for money in an emergency must say it.
  3. Urgency plus unusual payment is a red flag. Gift cards, crypto, wire transfers, or "don't tell anyone" mean stop and verify, every time.

The plan works because it doesn't depend on hearing whether the voice is fake. A cloned voice can be perfect; a scammer still can't answer from your son's real phone or know a word that was never written down.

#Exercise 3: Rank chatbot tasks by risk

Rank these from safest to riskiest, and say why:

  1. Brainstorm ten names for a robotics team.
  2. Summarize a paragraph you pasted in.
  3. List five books with page numbers to cite in a history essay.
  4. Tell you how much of a medicine to give a 6-year-old.
Need a hint?

Consider two things for each: how likely the chatbot is to invent something, and how bad it is if it does.

Show solution

From safest to riskiest: 1, 2, 3, 4.

  • Names have no right answer, so nothing can be false.
  • Summarizing your own text gives the model the facts, so it invents less, but it can still drop a "not" or blur a number. Skim it against the original.
  • Citations with page numbers are the most frequently invented output of all, as Mata v. Avianca showed. Every one needs checking.
  • A child's medicine dose combines a real chance of error with serious harm. Use the package label, a pharmacist, or a doctor, not a chatbot.

Risk is likelihood times harm, and number 4 is the only one where both are high.

#Exercise 4: The plant-watering idea

A classmate wants to train a machine learning model on photos of a houseplant to predict when it needs water, then send a reminder. Run the five questions. Does AI fit?

Need a hint?

Think about how a gardener actually decides when to water. Is there a simpler signal than a photo?

Show solution
Question Answer
Task Fairly clear: dry or not dry.
Data Needs many labelled photos of the same plant, wet and dry; that's weeks of collecting.
Stakes Low. A wrong guess means a slightly thirsty plant.
Errors Easy to notice and fix.
Alternatives A repeating reminder every few days, or a cheap soil moisture sensor, which measures dryness directly.

Verdict: not a good fit. A photo is an indirect clue about something you can measure directly. It's a fine learning project, but as a solution, a sensor or a calendar reminder beats it. "Could AI do this?" and "should AI do this?" are different questions.

#Exercise 5: The essay detector, by the numbers

A teacher runs 300 essays through a detector with the same accuracy OpenAI reported for its 2023 classifier: it flags 26% of AI-written essays and wrongly flags 9% of human-written ones. Suppose 30 of the essays were really AI-written. How many students get flagged, and how many of them did nothing wrong?

Need a hint?

Work with the two groups separately: 30 AI-written essays and 270 human-written ones. Apply the right percentage to each, then add up the flags.

Show solution

32 students are flagged and 24 of them wrote their own essays, while 22 of the 30 AI essays slip through. The detector is wrong about most of the people it accuses and misses most of what it's looking for. This is the rare-disease puzzle from Module 5 again: when the thing you're hunting is a minority, even a modest false-positive rate buries the real cases under false alarms.

#Exercise 6: Score three proposals

For each proposal, give a short answer to each of the five questions and a verdict: go, go with conditions, or don't.

  1. Sort photos of lost-and-found items into categories (jackets, bottles, phones) and post them on the school website.
  2. Predict which ninth graders will drop out, so counselors can reach out early.
  3. A chatbot that answers students' questions about the school handbook.
Need a hint?

For number 2, a real system already exists: Wisconsin's Dropout Early Warning System. A 2023 investigation by The Markup found that when it predicted a student wouldn't graduate on time, it was wrong nearly three-quarters of the time, and wrong more often for Black and Hispanic students than for white students.

Show solution

1. Lost-and-found sorter: go with conditions. The task is clear, the data is easy to collect, mistakes are cheap (a jacket filed under "bags"), and a person posts the photos. Conditions: blur or crop names, ID cards, and phone lock screens before posting, since the items often carry personal information.

2. Dropout prediction: don't, as proposed. The task sounds clear but the label (who drops out) depends on support students receive. Historical data reflects existing inequality. The stakes are high: a "high risk" label can change how adults treat a student. The Wisconsin case shows the errors are frequent and fall unevenly. Alternatives exist: counselors already watch attendance, grades, and behavior, which are direct and explainable. If a school insists, conditions would include never showing the score to teachers, testing error rates by group first, and using it only to offer help, never to restrict anything.

3. Handbook chatbot: go with conditions. The task has right answers (they're in the handbook), but chatbots invent rules, as Air Canada learned in court. Conditions: answers must quote and link the exact handbook section, the bot says "I don't know, ask the office" when the handbook doesn't cover something, and a person reviews a sample of answers each month. Also ask whether a well-organized, searchable handbook page would do the job with no AI at all.

#Challenge: Judge an AI feature you've used

Choose an AI feature you've actually used (autocorrect, a music or video recommendation feed, photo face grouping, a homework helper). Write one paragraph that answers the five questions and ends with a verdict: does AI fit this job, and what one change would make it safer or fairer?

Show solution

A model answer for photo face grouping (a phone's photo app that groups pictures by person):

The task is clear: decide whether two faces are the same person. The data is my own photo library, but the faces in it belong to friends and family who never agreed to be grouped. Stakes are low for me (a wrong group is easy to fix), and errors are visible and correctable by hand. The alternative, tagging people manually, works but takes much longer. Verdict: AI fits, because errors are cheap, visible, and fixable by the user. One change that would make it better: keep face grouping on the device and off by default, so people's faces aren't processed until the owner chooses it.

Your paragraph should name a real trade-off and a specific change. "It's good" or "it's creepy" without reasons isn't a verdict.

What you'll learn

  • Describe what the capstone produces: a recommendation memo, evidence, and a short presentation.
  • Choose a problem that is real, specific, and small enough to research well.
  • Map the people a system would affect, including people who are never asked.
  • Plan the evidence you'll gather: a prototype test, checked sources, or interviews.
  • Fill in a one-page plan for your recommendation.

Since 2012, a computer system in Wisconsin has scored every sixth through ninth grader in the state on how likely they are to graduate from high school on time. In 2023, the news site The Markup reported that when the system flagged a student as high risk, it was wrong nearly three-quarters of the time, and wrong more often for Black and Hispanic students than for white students. Somewhere, early on, someone wrote a recommendation saying this was a good idea.

Your capstone is to write that kind of recommendation, but well. You'll take a real proposal to use AI, investigate it with everything from this course (confidence, errors, bias, privacy, consent, misinformation, alternatives), and recommend what should happen. "Don't use AI here" is an allowed answer. So is "yes", if your evidence supports it.

#What you'll produce

Part What it is Built in
Recommendation memo 800 to 1,500 words, using the template in the next lesson Lesson 2
Evidence At least one of: a Teachable Machine prototype with a stress test, a verification log of claims about the system, or interviews with people affected Lesson 2
Presentation 3 minutes, with up to 5 slides or a one-page handout Lesson 3

Every memo ends with one of four verdicts:

  • Go: use AI as proposed.
  • Go with conditions: use it only if specific safeguards are in place, and name them.
  • Not yet: it might work, but something must be tested or fixed first.
  • Don't: AI is the wrong tool, and here's what to do instead.

#Five proposals to choose from

Each is a real kind of system that schools and organizations are offered or already use. They're listed from most straightforward to hardest to judge.

Level Proposal What makes it interesting Evidence you could gather
Starter Lost-and-found sorter. Photograph items handed in, sort them into categories, and post them online. Low stakes, but items carry names, ID cards, and phone screens. Teachable Machine image model of 3 or 4 item types, stress-tested on new items
Starter Cafeteria waste camera. Photograph trays at the return window to estimate how much food is thrown away. Useful data, but who appears in the photos? Image model with "mostly eaten / half / mostly left" classes
Intermediate Classroom noise monitor. An always-on microphone warns when the room is too loud. Privacy of constant listening, and a sound model that has to tell "talking" from "chairs scraping". Teachable Machine Audio Project (it needs at least 20 seconds of Background Noise)
Intermediate Handbook chatbot. Students ask questions about school rules and get instant answers. Hallucinated rules, as in the Air Canada case; students under 13 using it. A verification log of a chatbot's answers to 15 real handbook questions (if you're old enough to use one), or a review of how a similar bot behaved
Advanced Face recognition at the entrance, or dropout prediction to assign counselors. High stakes, real documented harms, consent problems, uneven errors. Published research (Gender Shades, The Markup's investigation), interviews, and a careful alternatives analysis. No prototype on real faces.

Or bring your own. A problem from your school, team, club, family business, library, or town is often the best choice, because you can talk to the people it affects. A good own-problem passes three tests: someone has actually proposed (or could reasonably propose) AI for it; you can find or create evidence about it; and it's narrow enough to cover in 1,500 words. "AI in healthcare" fails the third test. "An app that reads my grandmother's pill labels aloud" passes all three.

💡 Tip

Pick the problem you'd most like to argue about at dinner. You'll spend a few weeks with it, and caring about the answer shows in the writing.

#Map everyone it affects

Most bad AI decisions forget somebody. List three groups:

  1. Users: people who operate the system (the front office, the teacher, the student asking the chatbot).
  2. Subjects: people the system makes decisions about (the student flagged as high risk, the face at the door).
  3. Bystanders: people affected without being asked (visitors walking past a camera, a classmate whose voice the noise monitor records).

Subjects and bystanders are the ones whose voices go missing. In the Wisconsin case, the subjects were sixth to ninth graders, and students The Markup interviewed were surprised to learn the system existed at all.

#Talk to two or three of them

Nothing beats asking. A ten-minute conversation with someone affected often reveals the thing no article mentions. Useful questions:

  • How is this handled now, and what's frustrating about it?
  • If a system got it wrong about you, what would happen next? Who would you tell?
  • What would you want to know before agreeing to this?
  • Would you rather have this, or [the simple alternative]?

Ask permission before taking notes, and don't record names in your memo unless people agree. Your own data plan from Module 6 applies to your research too.

#Plan your evidence

Your memo needs at least one kind of evidence beyond your opinion:

  • A prototype test. Build a small Teachable Machine version and stress-test it like the rock-paper-scissors model in Module 5: conditions, groups, a log, a confusion matrix, and accuracy by condition. A prototype can't prove a real product works, but it can reveal how this kind of system fails.
  • A verification log. List the claims made for the system (a vendor's "99% accurate", a news story's numbers) and check each against original sources, as in Module 7.
  • Interviews with the people you mapped above, summarized without names.

Strong memos usually combine two of these.

#Fill in your plan

Copy this into a document and fill it in. It should fit on one page.

Writing down your first guess matters. At the end, compare it with your final verdict. If the evidence never moved you at all, ask yourself whether you really looked.

#A filled-in example

The next lesson follows this example through every milestone:

The plan already does something good: it spotted that the riskiest part isn't the AI at all. It's what's in the photos.

Key takeaways

  • The capstone is a recommendation, not a sales pitch. "Don't" and "Not yet" are real answers.
  • Choose a problem that is real, specific, and small enough to research properly.
  • Map users, subjects, and bystanders; subjects and bystanders are the ones most often forgotten.
  • Plan at least one kind of evidence beyond opinion: a prototype test, a verification log, or interviews.
  • Write down your first-guess verdict so you can see whether the evidence changed your mind.

#Further reading

  • AI Incident Database (opens in a new tab): thousands of reported cases where AI systems caused harm. Search it for systems like the one you chose.
  • The Markup's investigation of Wisconsin's dropout predictor (opens in a new tab): a model of how to investigate a real system, using public records, data, and interviews.

m8-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write each section of a recommendation memo from a starter template.
  • Turn prototype test results into a confusion matrix and accuracy-per-class chart.
  • Rank risks by likelihood and harm, and attach a safeguard to each.
  • Compare AI against non-AI alternatives on cost, privacy, and errors.
  • Write a verdict with conditions, an honest uncertainty statement, and what would change your mind.

Here's the skeleton your memo will grow from. Copy it into a document now. Each milestone below fills in one or two sections, using the lost-and-found example from the last lesson to show what a finished section looks like.

Work through the milestones in order. Each ends with a check: if you can't answer it, the section isn't done.

#Milestone 1: The problem and the people

Describe the problem without mentioning AI. If you can't, you may be starting from a solution looking for a problem.

Notice the evidence already in there: a number from the office, and what interviews found. That beats "lots of things get lost."

Check: Could someone who has never seen your school understand the problem from this paragraph alone?

#Milestone 2: The proposal, the data, and privacy

Say exactly what the AI would do and what happens with its output. Then summarize your data plan from Module 6 in a few lines.

Check: Does your data section say where data comes from, who agreed, and when it's deleted?

#Milestone 3: Gather the evidence

For the example, a student built a five-class Teachable Machine prototype, then tested it on 60 photos of items it had never seen: 12 per class, half on a plain desk and half on a cluttered one. They tallied each result into a grid. If you're using Colab, paste the cell below and replace the grid with your own counts. If not, your hand tally is the evidence; the chart just makes it easier to read.

Read it the way you learned in Module 5. Bottles and jackets are easy: they look alike within their class. Other is a coin flip at 50%, and its errors are scattered across every column. That makes sense: "Other" holds calculators, hats, lunchboxes, and glasses, which share nothing visual. And it's the category whose items are already hardest to find.

The student also split results by condition: 27 of 30 right on a plain desk (90%), 21 of 30 on a cluttered one (70%). Here's how that becomes memo text:

That last interview line turns out to matter more than the chart.

Check: Does your evidence section include numbers, say what they do and don't prove, and mention at least one surprise?

#Milestone 4: Rank the risks

List every risk you can think of across the course's themes (errors, bias, privacy, misinformation), then score each for likelihood and harm from 1 to 3:

# Risk Likely Harm Safeguard
1 A name or face visible on a posted item 3 2 Staff check and crop every photo before posting
2 A phone posted with notifications on its lock screen 2 3 Never photograph the screen side of a device
3 "Other" items filed in the wrong section 3 1 Post "Other" items in every section, or skip sorting them
4 Someone claims an item that isn't theirs 2 2 Owner must describe a detail not shown in the photo
5 Electronics posted as "Other" and missed 1 2 Staff review all electronics by hand

Look at which risks landed in orange. Both are about what's in the photos, and neither is caused by the AI. They'd exist with or without a model. The AI's own errors (risks 3 and 5) are real but low-harm. That's a finding worth stating plainly in your memo.

Check: Does every risk have a safeguard, and does every safeguard name who does it?

#Milestone 5: Compare the alternatives

Always compare at least three options, including one with no AI:

A. Staff sort by hand B. AI sorts, staff review C. AI sorts and posts automatically
Staff time per week About 15 minutes About 10 minutes About 5 minutes
Privacy check before posting Yes Yes No
Sorting errors Very few Few (staff catch them) 1 in 5 items, more for "Other"
Setup None Train and maintain a model Train and maintain a model
Solves the real problem? Yes: photos go online Yes Yes, with privacy risks

The table makes the uncomfortable point. The real problem was that students never saw the items; posting photos online fixes that. Sorting into categories is the small part, and people do it in seconds. Option B saves five minutes a week at the cost of building and maintaining a model. Option C saves more time but skips the privacy check that the risk map says matters most.

Check: Is there an option with no AI at all, and did you judge it fairly?

#Milestone 6: Write the verdict

Your verdict section has four parts: the verdict, its conditions, what would change your mind, and what you don't know.

The example's first guess was Go with conditions. The evidence moved it to Don't, not because the model was bad (80%, and 100% on bottles), but because the interviews and the alternatives table showed the AI wasn't solving the expensive part of the problem. That's what good evidence is supposed to do.

#Assemble the memo

Put the sections together, add a Sources list with links (the Teachable Machine FAQ, any articles or studies you used, and "interviews with three students and the office manager, October 2026"), then write the Summary last:

A reader who stops after the summary should still know your verdict and why.

Key takeaways

  • Describe the problem without mentioning AI. Then describe exactly what the AI would do and what its output decides.
  • Evidence means numbers with limits: say what your prototype shows and what it can't prove.
  • Score risks by likelihood times harm, and give each one a safeguard and an owner.
  • Always compare against a no-AI option. Sometimes it wins.
  • A verdict includes conditions, what would change your mind, and what you don't know.

#Further reading

  • Teachable Machine FAQ (opens in a new tab): cite it in your data and privacy section if your prototype used Teachable Machine.
  • AI Risk Management Framework (opens in a new tab): the US standards agency's guide to mapping and managing AI risks. Its Map, Measure, and Manage steps are the grown-up version of Milestone 4.

m8-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Test a recommendation by fact-checking it, arguing against it, and reading it as the person most affected.
  • Check that the memo answers every question this course has taught you to ask.
  • Present a verdict and its evidence clearly in three minutes.
  • Grade your work against a rubric and reflect on what changed your mind.
  • Pick a next step for learning more about AI.

In Module 5 you learned that a model which scores 100% on its own test can fall to 56% on someone else's hand. Your memo has the same weakness: it's been checked only by the person who wrote it. Before you present it, try to break it.

#Five tests for your memo

#Test 1: Fact-check yourself

Make a verification log of your own memo, exactly as in Module 7. Every number, name, date, quote, and study gets a row and a source. Then re-derive every number you calculated: if your memo says "75% of flagged students were innocent," redo the division.

Common finds: a statistic you remembered but can't trace, a percentage without its denominator, a quote you paraphrased into quotation marks. Fix or cut each one.

#Test 2: Let a partner argue the opposite

Give your memo to a partner. Their job is to argue for the opposite verdict for five minutes, as convincingly as they can. If you said "Don't," they argue "Go"; if you said "Go with conditions," they argue "Don't."

Write down every argument. For each one, either answer it in your memo or admit it in "What I don't know." An argument you can't answer and didn't mention is the weakest point in your work, and your audience will find it if you don't.

#Test 3: Read it as the person most affected

Reread the memo as one of your subjects or bystanders: the student who gets flagged, the visitor walking past the camera, the child whose voice is recorded. Ask:

  • Does the memo say what happens to me when the system is wrong?
  • Can I find out a decision was made about me, and can I appeal it to a person?
  • Did anyone ask for my consent, and could I say no without losing something?

If the memo is silent on any of these, add it. It's the part most professional proposals leave out.

#Test 4: The five-question audit

Check that your memo answers every question the course has taught you to ask. Mark each row with the section number where it's answered:

Question Where it's answered
Task: is there a checkable right answer?
Data: enough, representative, and consented?
Stakes: who is hurt by an error, and how badly?
Errors: what kinds (false positives, negatives), and are they spread evenly across groups?
Confidence: what happens when the system isn't sure?
Privacy: what's collected, where it goes, when it's deleted?
Misinformation: could it generate or spread false content?
Oversight: who reviews decisions, and how do people appeal?
Alternatives: was a no-AI option compared fairly?

Not every row needs a long answer. "Not applicable: the system generates no text" is a fine answer for misinformation in an image classifier. A blank is not.

#Test 5: The plain-language check

Read your summary to someone outside the course, such as a parent, a younger sibling, or a friend. Ask them to tell you the verdict and one reason. If they can't, rewrite the summary.

Swap jargon for plain words, or explain it the first time: "confusion matrix" becomes "a table of which items the model mixed up"; "false positive" becomes "a false alarm". Write numbers with their denominators: "8 of 12 bags" is clearer and more honest than "67%".

#Present in three minutes

Three minutes is short. Spend it on the verdict and the evidence, not on background.

Time Slide What to say
0:00 to 0:20 1. The problem One concrete story: "Last term, 300 items were donated because nobody knew they were found."
0:20 to 1:00 2. The proposal and the test What AI would do, and what evidence you gathered
1:00 to 2:00 3. What you found One chart, explained: the finding that most affected your verdict
2:00 to 2:40 4. The verdict Verdict plus conditions, in one sentence each
2:40 to 3:00 5. What would change my mind Your honest uncertainty

A few presenting habits help a lot. Say your verdict in the first minute and the last, because people remember beginnings and endings. Point at the part of the chart you're talking about. And practise out loud, with a timer, at least twice: almost everyone runs long the first time.

Prepare for the questions you'll probably get:

  • "Isn't the AI going to get better? Why not just wait?"
  • "What would it take for you to say yes?"
  • "Who did you actually talk to?"
  • "Your prototype isn't the real product, so how much does it prove?"

The last one is fair, and the best answer is honest: a prototype shows how this kind of system fails, not exactly how often the real one would.

#The rubric

Grade yourself first, then compare with your teacher's or a partner's grade. Each row is scored 1 to 4.

Criterion 1: Beginning 2: Developing 3: Strong 4: Excellent
Problem and people Problem described in terms of AI Problem clear; only users considered Problem clear; users and subjects mapped Users, subjects, and bystanders mapped; interviews inform the problem
Evidence Opinion only One source or test, numbers without limits Prototype, log, or interviews with numbers and stated limits Two kinds of evidence that agree or are reconciled; surprises reported
Errors and fairness Not discussed Overall accuracy only False positives and negatives named; one group comparison Errors split by group or condition; who bears them is explained
Privacy and consent Not discussed Mentions privacy generally Data, consent, and deletion addressed Data minimized; consent is real; quasi-identifiers and children's data handled
Alternatives and oversight None One alternative, not compared No-AI option compared fairly; human review described Several options compared on clear criteria; appeal path for affected people
Verdict and uncertainty No clear verdict Verdict without conditions Verdict with conditions and limits Conditions, what would change the verdict, and what's unknown all stated
Communication Hard to follow Clear but long or jargon-heavy Clear summary; charts captioned; sources listed A non-expert can state the verdict and a reason after the summary

A total of 21 or more out of 28 is strong work. A score of 4 on Verdict and uncertainty is worth more than the rest, because it's the skill most professionals still struggle with.

#Reflect

Write a short paragraph answering these. They're for you, not for a grade:

  1. What was your first-guess verdict in the planning lesson? Did it change, and what moved it?
  2. Which piece of evidence surprised you most?
  3. Which question from the course would you now ask about every AI system you meet?
  4. If you built this system for real, what's the first test you'd run?

#Where to go next

You can now judge AI systems better than many people who buy them. Here's how to keep going, depending on what you enjoyed:

  • You liked the charts and the "why" behind them. Learn Python next. Every chart in this course is a few lines of it, and Google Colab runs it for free in a browser.
  • You want to build real models. Once you know some Python, Google's Machine Learning Crash Course covers the ideas from this course (thresholds, confusion matrices, fairness) with code you run yourself.
  • You want the big picture without code. Elements of AI is a free online course from the University of Helsinki and MinnaLearn on what AI is and how it affects society.
  • You liked the investigations. Browse the AI Incident Database and pick a case. Try writing the recommendation someone should have written before that system launched.

Key takeaways

  • Test your memo like a model: fact-check it, have someone argue the opposite, and read it as the person it affects most.
  • Audit it against every question from the course; a blank is a gap, while "not applicable, because..." is an answer.
  • Write in plain language with numbers and their denominators.
  • In three minutes: one story, one chart, the verdict twice, and your honest uncertainty.
  • Good AI judgement is a habit: ask about task, data, stakes, errors, privacy, and alternatives every time.

#Further reading

  • Google's Machine Learning Crash Course (opens in a new tab): free lessons with interactive exercises, for when you're ready to build models with code.
  • Elements of AI (opens in a new tab): a free, non-technical course on what AI can and can't do, from the University of Helsinki.
  • AI Incident Database (opens in a new tab): real cases of AI systems going wrong, searchable by topic, for your next investigation.
